pages.title: The wrong classroom
pages.text:
So after a long time, we finally met. My one and only one, apdi nu dhaan solluven. Small correction: at the beginning of this story, I hadn't met him yet. 😔

I was Shreya, sixteen, Class Eleven, professional overthinker, occasional maths survivor. My idea of romance involved rain, a good soundtrack, and somebody understanding why the last piece of chocolate was emotionally important.

Real life gave me a leaking classroom and a teacher holding forty-seven wet library cards.

“Shreya,” Revathi ma'am said, “I need a favour.”

That was how the trouble started.

pages.title: The wrong classroom
pages.text:
The favour was supposed to take ten minutes. Carry the attendance register to the old reading room. Leave it on the desk. Return before chemistry.

Except the reading-room door was stuck, my shoelace was open, and a boy on the other side pulled exactly when I pushed.

I landed against a stack of dictionaries. He caught the top three before they hit my head.

“Usually people knock,” he said.

“Usually doors open. Idhu door-ah, entrance exam-ah?”

Ma'am appeared behind him. “Excellent. You've met your partner.”

Partner? For what? My funeral after chemistry attendance?

pages.title: The wrong classroom
pages.text:
He belonged to Class Ten. Fifteen years old. Exactly one year younger than me, as I would discover through an extremely unnecessary argument about birthday candles.

His name was on the register. I read it that afternoon. Let me be honest about that now: he wasn't a secret agent, and our school wasn't allergic to introductions.

But in these pages, I'm keeping that name folded away for a while.

First, you should meet the boy I met: ink on his thumb, one crooked shoelace, and the patience to rescue a dictionary before making fun of me.

pages.title: The wrong classroom
pages.text:
The monsoon had damaged the little neighbourhood reading centre our school supported. Revathi ma'am wanted two students to catalogue donated books and prepare a reading programme for younger children.

“Shreya writes well. You organise well,” she told him. “Work here after lunch, with the library staff. Tell your parents about Saturday sessions.”

I heard extra work. He heard books.

Enakku homework-ey podhum; ippo social service vera. I sighed as if ma'am had personally cancelled my retirement.

“Can we save the ones with torn covers?” he asked.

Ma'am smiled. “We can try.”

He picked up the ugliest book first.

For reasons I didn't examine, that annoyed me less than it should have.

pages.title: The wrong classroom
pages.text:
Our first disagreement concerned labels. I wanted blue for stories and yellow for reference. He wanted alphabetical order.

“Children don't enter a library thinking, today I feel like the letter P.”

“They can still find things alphabetically.”

“They can find joy in blue. Konjam imagination use pannu, please.”

He considered this with ridiculous seriousness. Then he divided the blue labels alphabetically.

Compromise looked suspiciously like neat handwriting.

When the bell rang, I discovered he'd put aside a dry notebook for me. My chemistry notes had been under the register during the rain.

“Blue,” he said. “For your tragic stories.”

pages.title: The wrong classroom
pages.text:
Nila, my best friend, met me outside chemistry with the expression of a television reporter at a crime scene.

“Why are you smiling?”

“I'm not.”

“Un face-ku andha information sollu first. It's smiling without permission.”

I explained the library, the door, the boy. She became interested at exactly the wrong word.

“One year younger, Shreya.”

“Yes. Not one century.”

Our teacher asked why we were whispering. Nila said we were discussing bonding.

Technically, chemistry. Morally, betrayal.

That evening I covered the dry notebook in brown paper. I wrote my name neatly, then wondered whether he'd notice.

pages.title: The wrong classroom
pages.text:
He noticed the crooked label instead.

“That's going to peel off.”

“Unakku vera velaiye illaya? Good afternoon to you too.”

He offered the glue. I refused out of dignity, then borrowed it when the label immediately peeled off.

We worked at opposite ends of a table while the librarian, Mrs. Mary, repaired bindings. Somewhere between adventure stories and atlases, he asked what I liked reading.

“Books where the girl has a personality outside the boy.”

“Good standard.”

“And where the boy is less irritating than you.”

He slid me a mystery novel. “Try this. The boy disappears in chapter two.”

pages.title: The wrong classroom
pages.text:
Saturday arrived with parental permission, two lunch boxes, and Nila volunteering because she enjoyed free entertainment.

At the reading centre, a little girl called Thara refused every book except one missing its ending.

“Someone tore out the last page,” she said, furious.

He sat on the floor a respectful distance away. “Shall we make another ending until we find it?”

Thara demanded a dragon, a bus conductor, and an apology.

He included all three.

I laughed so loudly the centre coordinator looked up.

He looked up too. Just once. Then he lost his place in the story.

pages.title: The wrong classroom
pages.text:
On the bus home, Nila took the window seat and promptly pretended to sleep. I stood beside the pole; he stood near the door with the donated books.

At a sharp turn, my pen rolled under a seat. He retrieved it without dropping the carton.

“Do you practise being useful?” I asked.

“Straight-ah thanks solla maatiya? Or is teasing your official language?”

“Romba thanks, your highness.”

That earned a smile I could still draw from memory, despite being terrible at drawing.

When I got down, he lifted the carton in farewell.

I nearly waved at the books.

pages.title: The wrong classroom
pages.text:
That night I opened the blue notebook to do chemistry. A scrap of paper fell out.

Not a love letter. Calm down. It was an inventory list.

At the bottom, below fourteen damaged picture books, someone had written: Find an ending for Thara.

I wrote beneath it: The dragon should apologise first.

Then I stared at my reply. Was that weird? Was replying to stationery an advanced symptom? Aiyo, Shreya. Oru paper-kitta poi ivlo scene-ah?

I put the scrap back before I could change my mind.

On Monday, the old reading room was locked.

A notice on the door said the project had been suspended.

pages.title: Things written in blue
pages.text:
“Suspended means postponed,” Nila said, reading over my shoulder. “It doesn't mean your boyfriend has been expelled.”

“He isn't my anything.”

“Seri, seri. Un alphabet consultant, then. Happy-ah?”

The school needed a safety inspection after another ceiling leak. Revathi ma'am moved the books to an unused staff workroom and assigned different lunch slots so students wouldn't crowd it.

I got Mondays and Wednesdays. He got Tuesdays and Thursdays.

An excellent system for the school.

A deeply irritating system for someone who had spent Sunday deciding how casually to return an inventory list.

pages.title: Things written in blue
pages.text:
Mrs. Mary became our unwilling postal service.

“Leave project notes in the blue folder,” she said. “Actual project notes. I have lived through enough adolescent handwriting.”

I left instructions about the labels and, at the bottom, the dragon's apology.

On Wednesday, his reply waited under a paper clip.

The dragon says sorry, but the bus conductor wants exact change.

I pressed my lips together so hard my face hurt.

Underneath, he had done every label exactly as we'd agreed.

Being listened to, I discovered, could be terribly inconvenient for a person's peace of mind.

pages.title: Things written in blue
pages.text:
Our notes became a small country with its own laws. Book counts first. Jokes below the line. No names in the jokes, because Mrs. Mary said she didn't need witnesses for her headache.

He drew a tiny umbrella beside books that needed drying.

I began calling him Umbrella Boy in my diary.

Very original, Shreya. Enna oru creativity. Literature departments everywhere were trembling.

At home, Amma asked whether the library project was going well.

“Fine.”

“Then why are you buttering an empty plate?”

I looked down. My toast was still in the toaster.

pages.title: Things written in blue
pages.text:
On Friday, both classes were called to the hall for a reading demonstration. He stood with his classmates near the stage.

I raised the blue folder. He touched two fingers to his forehead in a tiny salute.

Then a girl beside him adjusted his collar, and the entire imaginary orchestra in my head stopped playing.

She wore our school uniform and looked perfectly comfortable beside him.

I spent the demonstration writing exceptionally aggressive notes about punctuation.

When Nila asked what was wrong, I said nothing.

Nothing had somehow acquired a face, a braid, and excellent collar-adjusting privileges.

pages.title: Things written in blue
pages.text:
I could have asked him. Instead, I did what every sensible sixteen-year-old does: invented a complicated tragedy while arranging dictionaries.

My next project note contained no joke.

His reply contained a question mark beside the empty space.

On Wednesday he waited outside the staff workroom, in full view of Mrs. Mary.

“Did I miss a task?”

“No.”

“Did I upset you?”

That was worse. An actual question required an actual answer.

I said, “The girl at assembly.”

He blinked. “My cousin?”

Somewhere, the dictionaries were probably laughing at me.

pages.title: Things written in blue
pages.text:
Her name was Kavya. She had transferred that term, lived with his family during the week, and apparently considered his appearance a public responsibility.

“She was removing a price sticker,” he said. “New shirt.”

“Oh. Cousin-ah? Seri. Naan summa dhaan ketten.”

Nobody in the history of questions had asked less casually.

“Did you think she was doing surgery?”

“Podhum. Poi edhavadhu alphabetise pannu. Please.”

He did not tease me about what I had really meant. That small kindness made my embarrassment bearable.

Later, a note appeared in the folder.

Important update: no stickers remain.

I wrote back: Your medical recovery inspires us all.

The country reopened its borders.

pages.title: Things written in blue
pages.text:
The birthday argument happened over donated calendars.

He mentioned his birthday. I said that was impossible because it was mine.

“You don't own the date.”

“Naan first vandhen. Seniority-ku konjam respect kudu.”

“Exactly one year first.”

We compared the years printed on our school identity cards. Same day, same month, one year apart. I was sixteen; he was fifteen. Simple maths, unusually distracting consequences.

“Senior citizen,” he said.

“Respect your elders.”

“Would you like the chair?”

I threw a blue label at him.

It stuck to his sleeve. He left it there until lunch ended.

pages.title: Things written in blue
pages.text:
Revathi ma'am announced an interschool storytelling event. Our reading project could send a student-written story and a short performance.

Nila volunteered me before I had finished inhaling.

“He can handle sound,” ma'am added, looking at Umbrella Boy. “Only if your classwork is up to date.”

He nodded, but his fingers tightened on the folder.

Afterwards I asked whether he disliked stages.

“Stages are fine. Unexpected microphones, less fine.”

I didn't understand yet.

“All right,” I said. “We'll make nothing unexpected.”

It was my first promise to him. Small enough to keep, I hoped.

pages.title: Things written in blue
pages.text:
I wrote a story about a train that stopped for people who weren't ready to say goodbye. It was dramatic. There was weather. Nila accused me of personally overwatering Indian Railways.

He read quietly, then tapped one line.

“Why does the girl give up her ticket?”

“For love.”

“Could the boy buy another ticket instead?”

I stared at him.

“Avalukku oru dream irukku, illa?” he said. “She wanted to go somewhere. She should get to go.”

I crossed out the ending.

That evening I wrote a better one, and for the first time, the girl boarded the train.

pages.title: Things written in blue
pages.text:
The final script disappeared two days before submission.

My folder was on the workroom table. The inventory remained. The jokes remained. Twelve handwritten story pages were gone.

Mrs. Mary hadn't moved them. Nila hadn't borrowed them. Revathi ma'am asked us to check calmly before accusing anyone.

Then I saw a photograph in the class group: another student's entry, already submitted.

The title was different.

The opening sentence was mine.

Under the photograph, someone had commented that our library boy had helped prepare it.

For the first time, I wished I had never answered his note.

pages.title: The wrong version
pages.text:
At lunch I held out my phone like evidence in a courtroom.

“Did you give him my story?”

He read the screen. His expression changed.

“I typed a script for Dev. I didn't know it was yours.”

“You read mine.”

“Only the first draft. His opened in a classroom.”

The photograph showed the second page, cropped above the borrowed sentence. My anger had arrived before the facts, carrying a loudspeaker.

“Romba convenient-ah irukku,” I said, letting my hurt do all the talking.

He set the phone down carefully.

“Ask me again when you want an answer you haven't already decided.”

pages.title: The wrong version
pages.text:
I hated him for that sentence until approximately four o'clock, when I hated myself for needing it.

At home, I found photographs I'd taken of my draft to send Nila. The dates were clear. I sent them to Revathi ma'am with a factual explanation.

No accusations about motives. No dramatic status update. Amma sat beside me until I pressed send.

“You can be hurt and still be accurate,” she said.

I wanted her to say everybody else was terrible.

Parents are very unreliable when you need professional assistance with being unreasonable.

pages.title: The wrong version
pages.text:
Ma'am met us with Dev and Mrs. Mary the next afternoon. Dev admitted taking the loose pages to photocopy an example of structure. He'd returned them to the wrong cupboard, then kept more than structure in his entry.

He apologised without looking at me.

Umbrella Boy had typed only what Dev gave him. His file history showed the earlier opening.

The entry was withdrawn. Ma'am asked Dev to write a new piece and credit any help.

Cinema-la vara madhiri dramatic punishment edhuvum illa. There was no grand scene.

Just an embarrassed boy, a corrected mistake, and my own apology still waiting to be said.

pages.title: The wrong version
pages.text:
I found him beside the water cooler.

“I should have listened.”

“Yes.”

A terrible response. Accurate responses often are.

“I was scared someone had taken the only thing I was good at.”

He leaned against the wall, considering that.

“Pages-a eduthukkalam, Shreya. Un talent-a edukka mudiyadhu.” He said it simply, as if that was the one fact I shouldn't have doubted.

I looked down at my shoes.

“I'm sorry,” I said, without adding but.

He nodded. “Next time, ask first.”

“Next time, please don't speak like a very young headmaster.”

His mouth twitched.

Our friendship didn't magically repair itself. But it accepted the first careful stitch.

pages.title: The wrong version
pages.text:
We rebuilt the script over three lunches. I wrote. Nila performed unrequested voices. He recorded sound cues on the school's old laptop.

When the rehearsal microphone squealed, he went still.

Not irritated. Frightened.

I turned the volume down and asked if he wanted a break. He nodded once.

Outside, he watched the courtyard until his breathing settled.

“At my old school, I froze during a speech,” he said. “Someone shared the video.”

I waited.

“People kept playing it.”

For once, I had no joke ready. I was grateful for that.

pages.title: The wrong version
pages.text:
“Nee stage-ku poganum-nu avasiyam illa,” I said. “Only do the part you actually want.”

“I know. I still want to do sound.”

“Then we'll test it before everyone arrives.”

He looked relieved that I wasn't turning his fear into a motivational speech.

We wrote a cue list with backup options. If the sound failed, Nila would keep reading. If he needed to leave, a teacher would take over.

Practical things. Boring things, probably, in a cinema romance.

But when he returned to the rehearsal room beside me, I felt something warmer than butterflies.

I felt trusted.

pages.title: The wrong version
pages.text:
On competition morning, the school van refused to start.

Nila declared this sabotage by the universe. Revathi ma'am arranged another van. We arrived with eight minutes to spare and a box of props on my lap.

At the entrance, I tripped over my own shoelace again.

He looked at it, then at me.

“Recurring theme.”

“Idhu en signature entry. Character consistency.”

He held the props while I tied the lace properly.

Inside the hall, a hundred unfamiliar faces turned towards the stage.

His hand tightened on the cue sheet.

I pointed to our backup plan. He nodded and stepped forward.

pages.title: The wrong version
pages.text:
We did not win.

Please adjust the imaginary background music accordingly.

We came third. Nila skipped an entire paragraph, I dropped a cardboard station sign, and the final train whistle sounded suspiciously like a kettle.

But he managed every cue. When the applause came, he looked surprised by it.

I clapped for him until my palms stung.

On the way out, a judge stopped me. “Your ending lets the girl have a future. Keep that.”

I glanced at the boy carrying our ridiculous station sign.

“I will,” I said.

I meant more than the story.

pages.title: The wrong version
pages.text:
We shared a packet of biscuits in the van, passing it through Nila because she had appointed herself the international border.

“Ungala vechukittu mudiyala,” she said. “Please, just be normal for one biscuit packet.”

He offered me the last biscuit.

I broke it in half.

Such a tiny thing. No violins. No slow motion. Only crumbs on my skirt and afternoon traffic outside.

Yet I remembered how he'd wanted to save the torn books, how he had asked why my heroine must stay behind.

My heart, traitor that it was, quietly changed his classification.

Not just friend.

Oh, kadavule.

pages.title: The wrong version
pages.text:
Monday's note was waiting in the blue folder.

Thank you for making a plan instead of making a speech.

Below it sat a pressed yellow flower, flattened between two scraps of clean paper. Not a rose. Probably something he'd rescued from the courtyard.

I carried it home inside my notebook like a highly confidential national document.

That evening his class teacher posted an updated project rota.

His name was absent from every remaining Saturday.

I checked twice.

Then a message arrived from Kavya: If he seems distracted tomorrow, please don't take it personally.

pages.title: An empty chair
pages.text:
He wasn't at school the next day.

Or the next.

The blue folder stayed painfully organised. There were no new umbrellas in the margin, no complaints about my label spacing.

Kavya said there was a family situation, and I didn't push her for details. I asked whether I could send the homework through her.

“Please,” she said.

I copied the assignments carefully, then added a note on separate paper.

Reply panna vendam. First veetla ellam paathukko. Your alphabet is safe with me.

I erased a heart I hadn't meant to draw.

The little dent in the paper remained.

pages.title: An empty chair
pages.text:
On Friday, he returned with tired eyes and no lunch box.

I offered half of mine. He initially refused, then accepted when I said Amma had packed enough lemon rice to feed a cricket team.

“My mother had surgery,” he said quietly. “She's recovering. I'm helping at home.”

“Aunty recover aaguradhu romba santhosham. Nee saaptiya?” I asked, moving the lunch box between us.

He nodded, looking at the food.

I didn't say everything happened for a reason. I couldn't imagine a reason good enough to make his week necessary.

Instead, I passed the potato fry.

For that lunch, it was what I could give.

pages.title: An empty chair
pages.text:
The Saturdays he'd missed had become weekday chores: collecting groceries, helping his younger sister with homework, answering relatives who all wanted updates at once.

“Her name is Anu,” he said of his sister. “She's nine and thinks I'm a badly paid assistant.”

“You're paid?”

“In criticism.”

That sounded like a sibling.

He smiled properly for the first time that week.

I wanted to fix every difficult thing. Instead, I asked what project work he could reasonably manage.

“Don't give away my chair,” he said.

“I was considering renting it.”

“Terrible business plan. It wobbles.”

pages.title: An empty chair
pages.text:
Nila saw us sharing lunch and asked later whether we were together.

“No.”

“Do you want to be?”

I stared at the timetable as if it contained spiritual guidance.

“I don't know how to be somebody's girlfriend.”

“Adhukku certificate edhuvum thevai illa, madam. Most people learn as they go.”

“He has enough going on.”

“Then be his friend. That's not a waiting room.”

I looked at her.

Sometimes Nila said something so sensible that I worried she'd been replaced overnight.

We walked to class together. I put my arm through hers, and she let the subject rest.

pages.title: An empty chair
pages.text:
My first letter wasn't delivered.

It began, I like the way you remember small things, which sounded dangerously close to a complaint about surveillance.

The second version began, This is embarrassing, which was honest but lacked ambition.

The third simply said, I think about you when you're not here.

I folded it and hid it inside my story notebook.

Then Amma called me for dinner, and I spent twenty minutes discussing school fees while my entire emotional future sat beside an unfinished chemistry equation.

Being sixteen involved a truly unreasonable amount of multitasking.

pages.title: An empty chair
pages.text:
At the reading centre, Thara asked where her usual storyteller was.

“Helping his family,” I said.

“Then you do the dragon voice.”

My dragon sounded like an uncle with a sore throat. She accepted the effort and corrected the ending.

“Sorry sonna mattum podhuma?” Thara demanded. “The dragon can't keep doing it again.”

Mrs. Mary looked up from her book repairs. “An excellent editorial note.”

I wrote Thara's sentence in the project folder.

That evening I thought about apologies, including my own.

I decided the next time something frightened me, I would ask a question before inventing an answer.

pages.title: An empty chair
pages.text:
He read the folder on Monday and laughed at my description of the dragon's vocal difficulties.

Then he turned serious.

“Can I tell you something without you feeling you must fix it?”

I nodded.

His family was considering a move to his grandmother's town for a year. It would make his mother's recovery and the household expenses easier. Nothing was final.

The room seemed to tilt very slightly.

“Do you want to go?”

“I want everyone to be okay.”

“That wasn't what I asked.”

“I know,” he said. “It's the answer I have.”

pages.title: An empty chair
pages.text:
I cried on the bus home, quietly enough that the conductor asked whether I'd lost money.

“Something like that,” I said.

Nothing had happened. He hadn't left. We weren't together. I had no official reason to feel abandoned.

En manasukku indha logic ellam puriyala. My heart apparently did not require paperwork.

At home, I washed my face and helped Amma cut beans. She didn't interrogate me.

After a while she said, “You can tell me only the part you understand.”

So I told her about a friend who might move away.

She handed me a smaller knife and listened.

pages.title: An empty chair
pages.text:
Amma didn't promise that things would work out.

“You can care about someone without knowing where the story goes,” she said.

“Idhu romba kashtam, Amma. That sounds stressful.”

“It is.”

Very inspiring household. Five stars.

She nudged the bowl closer. “But don't punish them for a choice they may not have.”

The next morning I returned to the workroom with two sharpened pencils and my normal terrible handwriting.

We worked on the Saturday programme.

I didn't ask him to promise he would stay.

When our elbows touched over the book list, neither of us moved immediately.

pages.title: An empty chair
pages.text:
Revathi ma'am asked me to remain after the project meeting.

“I've recommended your writing for a residential summer workshop in Chennai,” she said. “There may be a fee waiver.”

For a moment, excitement beat everything else.

Then I looked through the window at the boy waiting near the courtyard.

A summer away. A possible move. Two directions opening at once.

Ma'am followed my glance but said only, “Take the form home. This is your decision with your family.”

I put it in the blue notebook.

Beside the letter I still hadn't delivered.

pages.title: The paper boat
pages.text:
“You should apply,” he said immediately.

I had shown him the workshop form hoping, embarrassingly, that he would look a little sad first.

“That's it?”

“What else?”

“Nothing.”

He studied me for a moment.

“Unna miss pannuven. Aana nee happy-ah irundha, enakkum santhosham dhaan. Those aren't opposite things.”

I became intensely interested in a glue stain.

“Who said you'd miss me?”

“I just did, Shreya.”

The way he said my name was unfair. Mine was available to him any time he wanted, while I could barely get an ordinary sentence past my own heartbeat.

pages.title: The paper boat
pages.text:
The application required a new story. I wrote about a girl who collected other people's unfinished goodbyes in a biscuit tin.

He didn't edit it for me. He read it and asked three questions, including why the girl never kept anything for herself.

I changed a scene. Nila corrected an unfortunate sentence that accidentally made the biscuit tin fall in love with a postman.

Amma signed the form.

Appa calculated the travel cost twice and said we would manage if the fee waiver came.

For once, my future felt like something several people were holding carefully.

pages.title: The paper boat
pages.text:
Our shared birthday fell on a school day.

I brought chocolates for my class and one extra packet of orange sweets, because he always traded for those.

He brought a bookmark he'd cut from sturdy card. On one side was a tiny umbrella. On the other: For stories with better endings.

“Senior discount?” I asked.

“Nee books-a konjam careful-ah handle panna, discount consider pannalam.”

I was seventeen now. He was sixteen. Still exactly one year apart, still equally incapable of saying the obvious.

Nila watched us exchange gifts and announced that she deserved cake for her suffering.

pages.title: The paper boat
pages.text:
The afternoon rain trapped us under the school verandah with half the building. Teachers called parents. Shoes squeaked. Somebody's tiffin leaked sambar into a bag.

He folded a scrap of unused paper into a boat.

“Super plan. Idhula rendu perum escape aagalam.”

“For your dramatic thoughts,” he said. “They need transport.”

I took it. Inside, beneath the crease, was a sentence.

I like the days you're in them.

I looked up.

He wasn't smiling now.

The rain made enough noise for every student on the verandah, but I heard only my own small inhale.

pages.title: The paper boat
pages.text:
“Project days?” I asked, because apparently I wanted romance delivered with an itemised invoice.

“Ella naalum, Shreya. Nee irukkura naal konjam nalla irukku.”

“Oh.”

He looked suddenly worried. “You don't have to answer now.”

I unfolded the boat carefully, smoothing the paper against my notebook.

“I like those days too.”

It was not an eloquent declaration. Nobody could frame it over a fireplace.

But his shoulders relaxed, and my face grew hot, and the world continued around us as if something enormous hadn't just become true.

Nila arrived holding three umbrellas.

“Why do you both look guilty of literature?” she asked.

pages.title: The paper boat
pages.text:
We didn't announce anything. We had a conversation, which turned out to be much harder than a dramatic confession.

“I want us to keep our friends,” I said.

“Yes.”

“Padippayum paakanum. Love vandhadhum chemistry-ku goodbye solla mudiyadhu.”

He laughed. “No messages when someone needs to work. No guessing games if we're upset.”

I looked meaningfully at the paper boat.

“That was one guessing game,” he admitted.

We agreed there was no rush to name everything.

Then the bell rang, and we went to different classrooms, both smiling like we had misread the timetable in a wonderful way.

pages.title: The paper boat
pages.text:
For one week, life became suspiciously kind.

He saved the seat closest to the fan. I remembered he hated coriander stems. Nila stopped teasing for almost forty minutes, a personal record.

At the centre, Thara asked why my dragon sounded happy.

“Improved working conditions,” I said.

He had to put down the book to laugh.

On Friday, we finished restoring our hundredth donated book. Mrs. Mary took a group photograph, making everybody hold a book instead of posing with empty hands.

I stood beside him.

Our little fingers brushed, and mine stayed there for a second.

pages.title: The paper boat
pages.text:
The workshop acceptance arrived on a Sunday.

Full fee waiver. Three weeks. My name typed correctly, which somehow made it more real.

I called Nila first because she would scream without asking sensible travel questions. Then I told my parents. Then I messaged him.

His reply came immediately: I knew your girl with the biscuit tin would make it.

A minute later: Proud of you.

I read those three words until the screen dimmed.

Then another message appeared.

Can we talk tomorrow? The move has been decided.

Happiness and dread sat down beside each other in my room.

pages.title: The paper boat
pages.text:
He would leave at the end of term. His mother was recovering steadily, but the family's plan made sense. His grandmother had space. His father's work could move. School admission was arranged.

I listened to all the sensible reasons and disliked every one.

“When?”

“The Saturday you leave for the workshop.”

Of course. Vera naale kedaikkalaya, universe? It enjoyed symmetry when it was being annoying.

“We can stay in touch,” I said.

“Yes.”

“Properly.”

“Yes.”

Neither of us knew yet how difficult properly could become when distance arrived with responsibilities, shared phones, and words that reached the wrong place.

pages.title: The paper boat
pages.text:
That night I took out the letter I'd hidden weeks earlier.

I think about you when you're not here.

It seemed too small now. I added a page about his patient silences, the repaired books, the way he had wanted my heroine to catch her train.

At the end I wrote: I like you. Not just the idea of you. The actual irritating person.

I signed it Shreya and drew one terrible umbrella.

The envelope was cream, borrowed from Appa's desk.

On the front, I wrote a private instruction: Open when you miss our wobbly chair.

pages.title: Promises at the gate
pages.text:
His farewell gift was a secondhand collection of short stories, repaired so carefully the spine opened without complaint.

“Page forty-two,” he said.

There was no hidden declaration. Only a story I'd mentioned wanting to read months earlier.

“You remembered?”

He looked almost offended. “You mentioned it three times.”

“Seri, statistics solli romance-a keduthudu. Very nice.”

Inside the cover, he'd written: Tell me which ending you would change.

I held the book against my chest.

I had planned to give him my letter then. Instead, Revathi ma'am called us to help pack the final donation box.

pages.title: Promises at the gate
pages.text:
The last school afternoon arrived too quickly. His parents needed him home early to finish packing, and my workshop train left the next morning.

We stood near the gate while teachers supervised dismissal.

“I have something for you,” I said.

“I have to run. Can you leave it with ma'am? Appa is collecting my certificate tomorrow.”

I wanted to demand five more minutes from the universe.

Instead, I nodded.

He held out his hand, tentative rather than certain.

I took it briefly.

“Nalla ezhudhu, Shreya,” he said. “And don't make your heroine miss that train.”

“Go miss our terrible chair.”

pages.title: Promises at the gate
pages.text:
I put the cream envelope into a large brown packet with the project photographs and his participation certificate. Revathi ma'am asked me to leave the packet on her desk.

“His father will collect it from the office,” she said.

I wrote his class on the outside. My hands shook absurdly for a person performing basic stationery work.

Before leaving, I looked at the workroom one last time.

The blue folder lay beside the repaired books. His chair stood slightly crooked.

I straightened it, then laughed at myself.

Love had apparently made me responsible for furniture alignment.

pages.title: Promises at the gate
pages.text:
The workshop train smelled of coffee and metal and possibilities.

I sent him a photograph of the window. He sent one of cardboard boxes stacked beside a suitcase.

Reached the station, I wrote.

Still searching for the tape, he replied.

We traded ordinary updates until his phone battery ran low.

I waited for a message about the letter.

By evening, there wasn't one.

Konjam time kudu, I told myself. People need time. Moving is tiring. Feelings don't come with guaranteed delivery notifications.

I placed his story collection beside my pillow and tried to sleep in an unfamiliar room.

pages.title: Promises at the gate
pages.text:
The first workshop exercise was to write a scene without explaining how anyone felt.

I wrote about a girl checking her phone under a table.

The instructor said the girl seemed anxious.

Excellent. At least somebody had received the message.

On the third day, he called for seven minutes. His mother was comfortable. Anu hated the new house's bathroom light. His grandmother was feeding everybody as if preparing for a famine.

“Did your father collect the packet?” I asked.

“Yes. The certificate's here.”

“And everything else?”

“I think so.”

The line broke before I could ask more.

pages.title: Promises at the gate
pages.text:
I sent a message: There was a cream envelope inside. For you.

It showed one tick for two days. When it finally delivered, no reply followed.

I wrote three increasingly dramatic follow-ups and deleted all of them.

At the workshop, my roommate Sana asked whether I was waiting for exam results.

“Something less organised.”

She gave me a guava slice and told me to come to the evening reading.

So I did.

For forty minutes, listening to someone else's story, I remembered that my own life contained more than a silent phone.

pages.title: Promises at the gate
pages.text:
His reply arrived on Thursday: I didn't find one. I'll ask Appa.

Relief hit first. Then embarrassment at the private trial I'd conducted without him.

It was a letter, I typed.

About?

Us.

The word looked enormous on the small screen. Namma rendu peru. Such a small phrase for so much hope.

Before he answered, a call came from Amma about train bookings. When I returned, he had written: Can we talk Sunday? I want to read it properly if we can find it.

Sunday felt far away, but it was a plan.

I saved my workshop notes and went downstairs for dinner.

pages.title: Promises at the gate
pages.text:
Sunday's call didn't happen.

His mother's follow-up appointment ran late. His phone was with his father, who needed it for directions. He sent an apology that night.

I believed him. I also felt disappointed. Both things fitted in the same chest, though not comfortably.

We rearranged for Tuesday.

Then my workshop group travelled to a village with almost no signal.

Distance wasn't a villain laughing from a balcony. It was appointments, weak batteries, borrowed phones, and two teenagers trying to sound less lonely than they were.

By the next week, we were both tired.

pages.title: Promises at the gate
pages.text:
When we finally spoke, I asked whether he had found the letter.

“No. Appa only remembers the certificate and photographs.”

“I can tell you what it said.”

A long pause. Somewhere behind him, Anu called for help with a school form.

“I like you,” he said softly. “That part hasn't changed. But everything here is unsettled. I can't promise constant calls.”

“Naan full day call panna sollala. Aana enna feel panren-nu enna ketkalam, illa?”

“I know. I'm scared of disappointing you.”

I stared at the hostel wall.

“You're doing it a little by deciding what I can handle.”

pages.title: Promises at the gate
pages.text:
He was quiet. Then he said, “You're right.”

We talked more honestly after that. One planned call each week when possible. A message if plans changed. Permission to say a week was difficult without proving it.

The letter could wait until the packet was found.

“Tell me one thing from it,” he asked.

I closed my eyes.

“I like the actual irritating person.”

He laughed, tired and familiar.

“Nalladhu,” he said. “Andha irritating person inga dhaan irukkaan. Still here.”

For that evening, it was enough.

I didn't know how much we would later ask those four words to carry.

pages.title: A letter without a home
pages.text:
Back at school, Class Twelve arrived like a relative who immediately asked about marks.

I had tests on Mondays, extra classes on Wednesdays, and a future everyone discussed as if it were a group project.

He entered Class Eleven in his new town.

Our Sunday calls became a small habit. Sometimes funny, sometimes awkward. Once we spent ten minutes trying to describe the same moon before realising he was looking at a streetlight through a tree.

“Un poetry career-ku inga full stop,” I told him.

“Please keep this confidential.”

Naturally, it is now in a book.

pages.title: A letter without a home
pages.text:
Revathi ma'am searched her cupboard for the missing envelope. The office had moved several project packets during repairs. Nobody remembered a cream letter specifically.

“I'm sorry, Shreya,” she said. “I should have handed the packet over myself.”

“You couldn't have known.”

She looked relieved that I wasn't asking her to become a detective in addition to teaching six classes.

I rewrote pieces of the letter in my diary, but sending a replacement felt strangely difficult.

The original belonged to the girl at the gate.

I was already becoming someone else, and I didn't yet know her handwriting.

pages.title: A letter without a home
pages.text:
A photograph upset me in September.

He stood with a girl at a science fair, both holding the same prize. She had tagged him with a heart and the words my favourite person.

Old Shreya began preparing a courtroom.

New Shreya asked him directly.

“That's Meera, my lab partner,” he said. “She's dating our team captain. That caption is on all four photos.”

I checked. It was.

“Naan thirumbavum overthink pannitten. Sorry,” I said.

“For asking? Don't be.”

I put down the phone feeling silly but lighter.

Progress, apparently, sometimes looked exactly like not ruining a perfectly ordinary evening.

pages.title: A letter without a home
pages.text:
He asked about my workshop friend Sana after seeing her comment on my story.

I told him everything: her excellent jokes, terrible alarm tone, and ambition to make documentaries.

“I like knowing who your people are,” he said.

My people. Such a comfortable phrase.

I told him about Nila's exam anxiety too, with her permission. He suggested a silly study scoreboard, which Nila accepted only because she could award penalties for our bad jokes.

We were not becoming each other's whole world.

We were learning the roads through the worlds we already had.

pages.title: A letter without a home
pages.text:
Then Appa lost a contract, and our house grew careful.

Careful shopping. Careful conversations. Careful silence whenever the phone rang.

I considered dropping my college applications outside our city. Train tickets and hostel fees suddenly looked enormous.

When I told him, he didn't say follow your dreams as if dreams paid deposits.

“First scholarships paakalam. Oru vazhi irukkum,” he said.

We made a list. Nila found deadlines. Revathi ma'am checked my essays.

Love, that week, looked like a spreadsheet I didn't hate.

For a person who had expected rain songs, this was a surprising development.

pages.title: A letter without a home
pages.text:
His birthday call came at midnight, on our shared birthday. I was eighteen; he was seventeen.

“Congratulations on legal adulthood,” he said. “Will your handwriting improve?”

“Respect your elders. It's tradition.”

He had recorded Thara's dragon story, with permission from the centre, giving the bus conductor a spectacularly tired voice.

I listened with my hand over my mouth so I wouldn't wake Amma laughing.

My gift was a story where the boy with a microphone got to choose when he spoke.

He went quiet after reading it.

Then he said, “You remembered the important bit.”

pages.title: A letter without a home
pages.text:
The difficult part began during exams.

We missed a call. Then another. He sent short messages because his father had started working nights and he was helping more at home.

I replied shortly because I was frightened about marks and money.

Nothing was technically cruel. Everything was slightly sharp.

One Sunday I said, “I can't keep being the only one waiting.”

He answered, “I was waiting last week.”

Rendu perum right dhaan. Aana rendu perum pesinadhu rendu different Sundays pathi.

Neither of us noticed.

When the call ended, I had the awful sense of a door closing without anyone choosing to shut it.

pages.title: A letter without a home
pages.text:
We tried again two days later.

“I care about you,” he said. “But I'm not doing this well.”

“Neither am I.”

We agreed to pause the expectations of a relationship through exams. We could send a message, but neither had to keep a weekly appointment. After results, we would talk honestly about what we wanted.

Indha mature conversation ellam enakku pudikkala. I wanted a much less mature miracle: him at the gate, telling me everything would somehow be easy.

Still, I wrote the agreement down so I wouldn't turn it into something harsher later.

A pause wasn't a punishment.

It also wasn't painless.

pages.title: A letter without a home
pages.text:
My scholarship interview happened on a rainy Tuesday.

Before leaving, I found a message from him.

Your heroine gets on the train. Remember?

I did.

At the interview, my hands shook until someone asked about the reading centre. Then I spoke about Thara demanding better endings, about damaged books, about children who needed stories that made room for them.

For ten minutes, I forgot to be afraid.

Outside, I sent him one message: I got on.

He replied with a little umbrella.

I put my phone away before I could ask what it meant for us.

pages.title: A letter without a home
pages.text:
The scholarship offer arrived after board results. Enough support to make Chennai possible. Appa read the letter twice, then hugged me so suddenly I nearly swallowed a laugh.

I called the boy that evening, as we'd planned after exams.

We were proud of each other. We were also exhausted by waiting for a future we couldn't describe.

“Ippo friends-ah iruppom,” I said, my voice shaking. “Later enna aagum-nu ippo promise panna vendam.”

He breathed out slowly. “Maybe.”

It hurt because nobody had stopped caring.

I packed his bookmark with my college things.

Some endings do not sound like doors. They sound like careful voices.

pages.title: The life between
pages.text:
College was louder than heartbreak.

There were hostel rules, new notebooks, a canteen serving coffee strong enough to argue back, and Sana waving across the courtyard because she'd joined a nearby film course.

Nila studied in our hometown. We called every Thursday and pretended not to miss sharing lunch.

Avana marakkala. But slowly, avan mattum dhaan en world-nu ninaikkuradhai vittuten. I simply gained other things to think about.

The first story I published in the college magazine wasn't romantic. It was about Amma bargaining with a vegetable seller who secretly saved the best beans for her.

She demanded royalties in phone calls.

pages.title: The life between
pages.text:
He sent congratulations when the story appeared online.

I replied with genuine warmth, then spent twenty minutes deciding whether genuine warmth had used too many exclamation marks.

Healing was not a smooth, tasteful montage.

Some days I missed him fiercely. Other days I realised at dinner that I hadn't thought about him since morning and felt inexplicably disloyal.

Sana said, “You're allowed to have a Tuesday.”

So I began allowing Tuesdays. Ordinary lectures. Laundry. A badly made omelette.

Slowly, my life stopped waiting at the window, even though part of my heart still liked the view.

pages.title: The life between
pages.text:
A classmate named Rohan asked me for coffee.

He was kind, funny, and capable of returning a borrowed pen without making it a personality trait. I said yes.

We talked about films and hometowns. Halfway through, I realised I was comparing his laugh with someone else's.

That wasn't fair to him.

Before a second date, I told him I wasn't ready for anything romantic.

He nodded. “Parava illa, Shreya. Coffee can still be coffee.”

We became friends eventually, without him waiting for a reward.

I appreciated that more than I knew how to explain at nineteen.

pages.title: The life between
pages.text:
On our next shared birthday, I turned nineteen and he turned eighteen.

His message arrived in the morning, simple and kind. Mine wished him good exams and a less terrible cricket team.

No midnight call. No hidden test.

I bought myself a slice of chocolate cake and called home.

Later, while cleaning my desk, I found the flattened yellow flower inside the blue notebook. Its colour had faded to a soft brown.

I didn't throw it away.

I also didn't spend the evening staring at it.

I slid it between clean pages and went out with Sana.

pages.title: The life between
pages.text:
Revathi ma'am phoned in December.

The neighbourhood reading centre had lost its lease. Volunteers were trying to relocate the books, and the school planned a small fundraising reading during the holidays.

“Would you contribute a piece?”

“Yes,” I said before she finished.

She asked if I could come in person. I checked my travel dates.

“I think so.”

After the call, a new volunteer group appeared on my phone.

Mrs. Mary. Nila. Kavya. Several parents.

And him.

My thumb hovered over his profile picture, then moved away.

I had agreed to help a library. I reminded myself of that twice.

pages.title: The life between
pages.text:
The group was practical. Transport quotes. Shelf measurements. Who could collect cartons.

He volunteered to repair the centre's old audio equipment. Apparently he had learned more sound work during his final school year and planned to study electronics.

I volunteered to edit the fundraising programme.

Nila messaged privately: Are you okay with seeing him?

I appreciated that she asked before making a joke.

I think so. Konjam nervous-ah irukku, I wrote.

Not the most confident sentence in human history. Still, it was true enough to begin with.

I booked a train home and placed the blue notebook in my bag.

pages.title: The life between
pages.text:
At home, the street looked smaller than I remembered. Amma said I'd grown taller. Appa said the street hadn't submitted a measurement report.

We ate dosa while I described college. For once, nobody asked about marks first.

Later I walked past school with Nila.

“Do you want a dramatic reunion?” she asked.

“No.”

She raised an eyebrow.

“Seri, konjam. Aana lighting nalla irukkanum.”

Nila laughed, then squeezed my hand.

“You don't have to become the old version of yourself just because you're going to an old place.”

I kept that sentence with me.

pages.title: The life between
pages.text:
The first volunteer meeting was in the same workroom.

The wobbly chair had finally been repaired. This felt like a personal betrayal by time.

He wasn't there yet. I helped Mrs. Mary sort old project records while Nila counted donated notebooks.

A carton from the office cupboard contained faded posters, spare certificates, and a large brown packet.

My handwriting was on the front.

I knew it before I lifted the flap.

Inside were duplicate photographs and a cream envelope, still sealed.

Open when you miss our wobbly chair.

For a moment, the room and all its sounds moved far away.

pages.title: The life between
pages.text:
Mrs. Mary checked the office label. Two nearly identical packets had been prepared that year: one to collect, one for the project archive.

Mine had gone into the archive carton by mistake. His father had collected the other.

No interception. No secret villain. Just a hurried office, matching brown paper, and a letter travelling nowhere for two years.

“I am so sorry,” she said.

I sat in the repaired chair.

“It wasn't your fault alone.”

What frightened me was how ordinary the answer was.

Idhukku dhaan ivlo azhudhen-ah? Something that had felt like fate had been a filing error.

pages.title: The life between
pages.text:
I held the unopened envelope while Nila quietly asked whether I wanted privacy.

“I don't know what to do with it.”

“You don't have to decide right now.”

So I put it in my bag. The choice, for the first time in years, was mine again.

A scooter stopped outside. Someone laughed in the corridor.

I recognised the laugh before I saw him.

Ridiculous, isn't it? Two years, new cities, different haircuts, and the heart still behaved like a dog hearing its favourite gate.

He entered carrying a box of cables.

Then he saw me.

pages.title: A familiar stranger
pages.text:
“Hi, Shreya.”

“Hi. Eppadi irukka?”

Simple question. En heartbeat mattum yen ivlo overacting pannudhu?

A magnificent reunion script. We should have hired writers.

He was taller, his hair shorter, his expression both familiar and difficult to read. At nineteen, I suddenly remembered every embarrassing thing I'd done at sixteen.

He set down the cables.

“How's Chennai?”

“Loud. How's home?”

“Also loud. Anu learned the recorder.”

I laughed before I could protect myself.

His face relaxed.

Around us, the project continued. Nila dragged a carton with unnecessary determination, generously pretending the room did not contain two people relearning how to stand near each other.

pages.title: A familiar stranger
pages.text:
We were assigned separate tasks by people who had actual work to finish.

I interviewed former reading-centre children for the programme, with their parents' permission. He tested speakers with a teacher supervising the hall.

Every so often, sound drifted through the corridor: a chord, a click, his voice counting softly.

He didn't freeze when the microphone crackled. He adjusted the cable and tried again.

I was happy for him in a way that didn't ask to be included in the achievement.

That feeling was new.

Later he caught me watching and lifted one eyebrow.

“Summa sound check,” I said. “Unna paakala. Professional assessment.”

pages.title: A familiar stranger
pages.text:
At tea break, he asked about the story I'd published about Amma.

“You read that?”

“Of course.”

“I thought you might just have seen the announcement.”

He quoted the vegetable seller's final joke, slightly wrong.

I corrected him automatically.

“There she is,” he said.

I looked away, smiling despite myself.

Then I remembered the envelope in my bag.

“I found something today.”

Before I could continue, Mrs. Mary called us to help move a shelf away from a damp wall.

I stood up.

This time, I promised myself, an interruption would remain an interruption. Not a whole ending.

pages.title: A familiar stranger
pages.text:
After the meeting, I asked him to walk to the gate with me. Nila waited nearby for our bus.

“The letter,” I said. “It was in the archive packet.”

He stopped.

“All this time?”

I nodded.

“Did you open it?”

“No. I wrote it. I know the embarrassing parts.”

He smiled briefly, then grew serious.

“Do you still want me to read it?”

That question undid me more than any automatic reaching hand could have.

“Konjam yosikkanum,” I said. “This time I want to understand my own answer.”

“Okay.”

He meant it. No pressure, no disappointed performance.

I took the bus home holding my bag carefully.

pages.title: A familiar stranger
pages.text:
That night, I opened my own letter.

The girl who wrote it was braver and more frightened than I remembered. She loved ink-stained fingers, ridiculous jokes, and a boy who listened.

She also thought distance was something two people could defeat by caring enough.

I wanted to hug her. I wanted to explain phone plans and exam timetables. I wanted to tell her none of what followed made her foolish.

At the bottom, the terrible umbrella leaned sideways.

I wrote a new date beneath the old one.

Then I took out a clean sheet of paper.

pages.title: A familiar stranger
pages.text:
The new letter was shorter.

I found this today. It belongs to who we were, and I'd like you to have it. You don't owe that version of me a reply. If we talk about us, let's talk as the people we are now.

I read it aloud once. No accidental biscuit-tin romance. Good.

The next afternoon, I handed both pages to him in the courtyard.

“Indha thadava un kai-la direct-ah,” I said. “Proper delivery.”

He accepted the envelope with both hands.

“I'll read it tonight.”

I nodded and returned to my editing table before I could supervise his feelings.

pages.title: A familiar stranger
pages.text:
His message came at ten.

I read both letters. Thank you for trusting me with them. Can we talk tomorrow after the meeting?

Yes, I wrote.

Then I put the phone down, picked it up, and put it down again.

Amma looked over her glasses.

“Is that device being difficult?”

“Extremely.”

“Tea?”

“Yes.”

We sat together without a speech. She asked about the library fundraiser. I told her about the missing lease and our plan for donated shelves.

By the time my tea cooled, I could breathe normally again.

Mostly. Let's not exaggerate my progress.

pages.title: A familiar stranger
pages.text:
He waited by the repaired chair after everyone packed up.

“I wish I'd read it then,” he said.

“Me too.”

“But it wouldn't have fixed every hard thing.”

I looked at him. I'd needed that sentence even though part of me wanted a prettier one.

“I know.”

He rubbed his thumb along the chair's edge.

“Un mela irundha care pogala, Shreya. I still care. But when I felt I was failing, I avoided the conversations that mattered.”

“I filled silences with the worst answer.”

We sat with those truths for a moment.

Nobody won. It felt better than winning.

pages.title: A familiar stranger
pages.text:
“Are you seeing someone?” he asked.

“No. You?”

“No.”

Two small answers, suddenly creating a great deal of space.

“I don't want to start again because a lost letter makes a good story,” I said.

“Neither do I.”

“I'd like to know you now.”

He nodded slowly. “Coffee after the fundraiser?”

“A conversation. Not a promise about our entire future.”

“Oru coffee-ku ivlo terms and conditions-ah?”

I laughed.

From the corridor, Nila called that our bus would not wait for character development.

We stood up together, and this time goodbye had an actual date attached.

pages.title: A familiar stranger
pages.text:
The next twist arrived from the centre's landlord.

The building had a buyer. We had ten days to clear the books, not the month we'd expected.

Mrs. Mary read the message aloud. The room fell silent.

Our fundraiser was scheduled for the following week. Even if it succeeded, we had nowhere ready to put the shelves.

He opened a notebook. Nila called the transport volunteer. I asked ma'am whether the school could store boxes temporarily.

Whatever happened between us would have to wait a little.

There were children about to lose a library.

This time, waiting had a clear reason.

pages.title: One hundred almosts
pages.text:
The school offered a dry storeroom for three weeks. Enough time to save the books, though not to reopen the centre.

We formed teams with adult volunteers. No heroic midnight trespassing. Just people carrying boxes after work, sweating through ordinary kindness.

He labelled every carton by section and alphabet.

I added blue stickers to the stories.

He looked at the familiar combination and smiled.

“Still a good system.”

“Obviously. Blue-na happiness-nu first sonnadhu naan dhaan.”

A child asked why we were laughing at labels.

Some explanations would have required an unreasonable number of pages.

pages.title: One hundred almosts
pages.text:
Dev arrived on the second packing day.

I hadn't seen him since school. He introduced himself to the coordinator and offered his family's small goods vehicle for transport.

“I wanted to help,” he said, looking at me. “Also, I still feel bad about the script.”

“You apologised.”

“I know. I'm not asking again.”

He carried the heaviest carton without turning it into a gesture.

Later, I watched him carefully write my credit under a programme excerpt.

People could become better in quiet ways. I was glad the story had room for that too.

pages.title: One hundred almosts
pages.text:
The fundraiser's guest reader cancelled because of a family emergency.

Revathi ma'am asked whether I could read my own piece instead.

In school, Nila had performed our stories. I wrote them from the safe side of the stage.

My first instinct was to refuse.

He didn't say I had to be brave. He asked whether I wanted to do it, underneath the fear.

“Yes,” I admitted.

“Appo oru plan pannalam. Naan inga dhaan irukken.”

The sentence returned to me from an old corridor.

We tested the microphone before anyone arrived.

Nothing unexpected, as far as care could arrange it.

pages.title: One hundred almosts
pages.text:
Nila rehearsed with me while he set sound levels. She stopped me whenever I rushed a sentence.

“Konjam slow-ah, madam express train. People need time to feel things.”

The piece was about the reading centre, not us. It began with a child refusing a book because somebody had stolen its ending.

At the back of the hall, he looked up.

I read the dragon's apology in my terrible voice.

He laughed so suddenly the microphone picked it up.

For the first time all afternoon, I forgot to fear the room.

I started again, slower.

pages.title: One hundred almosts
pages.text:
Fundraiser morning brought a new offer: a community hall could host weekend reading sessions for six months, if we covered transport and storage.

It wasn't a permanent home. It was a beginning we could afford if the event went well.

We updated the programme to explain exactly what donations would support. Mrs. Mary checked every figure.

No exaggerated promises about saving everything forever.

Before doors opened, he handed me a glass of water.

“Your story can be enough without doing everything,” he said.

I drank, nodding.

Then the first families arrived, and the hall became real.

pages.title: One hundred almosts
pages.text:
My hands shook when I stepped to the microphone.

I could see Amma and Appa in the third row. Nila stood beside the stage. Thara, older now, sat near the front with a book on her knees.

I began too fast. Stopped. Took a breath.

“I've waited a long time to tell this properly,” I said, and started again.

At the sound desk, he gave a small nod.

By the second paragraph, I was inside the story.

The room didn't disappear. It listened.

That turned out to be better.

pages.title: One hundred almosts
pages.text:
When I finished, Thara raised her hand.

“Can the dragon visit the new place too?”

The hall laughed gently.

“Varuvaan,” I said. “Avanukku ippo bus pass irukku.”

People stayed to ask about volunteering. Donations arrived in small amounts, mostly. Enough together to cover the first stage of the move.

Mrs. Mary cried while pretending to clean her glasses.

He helped a little boy reach the donation receipt box, then looked across the hall at me.

His smile was proud and open.

I didn't have to guess what it meant.

pages.title: One hundred almosts
pages.text:
We packed the chairs after everyone left.

Nila whispered, “Coffee. Tomorrow. Don't invent another administrative disaster.”

“I'll check with the universe.”

He walked over carrying the final microphone stand.

“Tomorrow at four? The café beside the bus stop.”

“Yes.”

“I'll be there.”

He said it simply, without making forever out of an afternoon.

At home, I chose an outfit, rejected it, and chose the same one again. Very efficient.

Inside my book, the old umbrella bookmark waited.

I took it out and put it in my bag for no practical reason whatsoever.

pages.title: One hundred almosts
pages.text:
I reached the café at three fifty.

Obviously, I told myself, this was about punctuality. Nothing to do with nerves. En heart-ku sudden-ah fitness mela interest vandhuduchu. It was running a marathon for completely unrelated reasons.

Rain dotted the window. The table wobbled very slightly.

I laughed before he arrived.

At four exactly, the door opened and he stepped inside, shaking water from an umbrella.

“Some things don't change,” I said.

“Your chair complaints?”

“Your weather accessories.”

He sat across from me. For once there were no books to catalogue, no bells, no teacher waiting for a report.

Only us.

pages.title: One hundred almosts
pages.text:
I have called him Umbrella Boy through a hundred pages. Not because I didn't know his name, but because a name alone couldn't tell you why he mattered.

Now you've seen the mistakes too. The silences. The kindness that didn't solve everything. The growing up we had to do separately.

At the café, he asked whether we could begin with an ordinary introduction. No pretending the past hadn't happened. Just room for who we'd become.

I held out my hand, smiling.

“Hi. I'm Shreya. Thirumbavum meet pannalama?”

He took it gently.

And this time, I'll let you hear what he said.

pages.title: Hello, again
pages.text:
“I'm Aadhav,” he said.

Aadhav.

There. The name I'd known since a wet attendance register, the name I'd written on an envelope and avoided saying too softly around Nila.

Across the café table, he smiled as though introducing himself to me was both ridiculous and worth doing properly.

“Nice to meet you, Aadhav.”

“You too, Shreya. I've heard you're very strict about library labels.”

“Only with difficult people.”

He laughed, and I let the name settle where it belonged.

Not as the answer to every question.

As the beginning of a conversation we were finally ready to have.

pages.title: Hello, again
pages.text:
We ordered coffee. Mine arrived too hot; his arrived with sugar he'd asked to leave out.

The waiter apologised. Aadhav thanked him for replacing it without making an audience of the mistake.

Idhellam enakku appove pudichirundhadhu. Adhukku love-nu peru irukku-nu dhaan konjam late-ah purinjadhu.

“Tell me something I don't know about you now,” I said.

He considered.

“I like working with sound more than I expected. Electronics feels like a way to understand it properly.”

“Music?”

“Music, recordings, spaces where people can hear each other.”

He looked almost shy about wanting something that clearly belonged to him.

pages.title: Hello, again
pages.text:
I told him I wanted to write books for young readers and work in publishing. Saying it outside an interview made it feel more fragile.

“Not the biscuit tin sequel?” he asked.

“That remains a commercial possibility.”

He smiled, then asked what the work actually involved.

We talked about editing, internships, fees, and whether I could tolerate a city where everybody seemed to walk faster than me.

He didn't treat my ambition as a charming hobby beside a more important life.

He asked questions as if he expected it to become real.

I wanted to do the same for him.

pages.title: Hello, again
pages.text:
“Are we trying again?” he asked eventually.

I watched rain slide down the glass.

“Thirumbavum try pannalaam. Aana slow-ah,” I said. “We can't promise distance will suddenly be easy.”

“No.”

“And if something isn't working, we say so before we disappear into politeness.”

Aadhav nodded. “I can do better at that.”

“So can I.”

He held his hand near mine on the table, leaving the last small distance for me to choose.

I crossed it.

Our fingers fitted without solving anything practical.

Still, my coffee had cooled, and his hand was warm, and I felt beautifully present.

pages.title: Hello, again
pages.text:
Nila demanded a report that evening.

“We had coffee.”

“Groundbreaking.”

“Pesinom, Nila. Proper-ah pesinom. Happy-ah?”

“Nobel committee notified.”

“We're trying again.”

She went quiet for a second. Then her voice softened.

“Are you happy?”

“Yes. And nervous.”

“Good. The nervous part can remind you to use actual sentences.”

I laughed.

She didn't ask for every private detail, and I didn't give them. Some moments belonged to Aadhav and me even in a friendship as close as ours.

After we hung up, I messaged him: Reached home. Coffee was a good beginning.

His reply: Next time, less sugar drama.

pages.title: Hello, again
pages.text:
Before I returned to Chennai, Aadhav met Amma and Appa properly.

They already remembered him from the reading project. This time I introduced him as someone I cared about and was getting to know again.

Appa asked about college. Amma asked after his mother. Aadhav answered without trying to become a different person for their approval.

When he left, Appa said, “He listens before answering.”

“That isn't a competitive exam skill, Appa.”

“It helps in several situations.”

Amma looked at me. “Take your time.”

For once, advice matched what I actually wanted.

pages.title: Hello, again
pages.text:
I visited his family the next afternoon with Amma, carrying fruit and an unreasonable amount of nervous energy.

His mother, Lakshmi aunty, looked well. She remembered the homework I'd sent during her recovery.

Anu, now twelve, informed me that Aadhav still lost socks and sang badly while washing dishes.

“Idhu romba useful information,” I said. “Innum enna secrets irukku?”

Aadhav looked betrayed by his entire household.

Kavya arrived midway through tea and immediately checked his collar for stickers.

I laughed so hard I had to explain the old misunderstanding.

By the end, the room felt less like an examination and more like a room.

pages.title: Hello, again
pages.text:
At the bus stop, Aadhav handed me the umbrella bookmark.

“You left it on our table.”

“I was pretending to be casual.”

“An ambitious project.”

I put it safely in my book.

He asked before hugging me. I said yes.

The hug was brief, warm, and slightly awkward because my bag got between us. We laughed, adjusted, and tried again.

No perfect choreography. Just two people making room.

When my bus arrived, he stepped back so I could board.

I found a window seat and waved.

This time, I was certain I was waving at him.

pages.title: Hello, again
pages.text:
Back in Chennai, we chose a weekly call time that actually fitted our schedules. If a week changed, we would reschedule without turning inconvenience into a verdict.

We also kept some calls short on purpose.

Ten minutes about dinner could be better than two exhausted hours trying to prove devotion.

“Today I have nothing interesting,” I warned one evening.

“Boring-ah irundhaalum sollu. Un day pathi kekkanum.”

“My laundry dried.”

“Excellent news. National importance.”

I laughed into my pillow.

Little by little, the relationship stopped feeling like an exam we could fail by saying the wrong thing.

pages.title: Hello, again
pages.text:
A month later, Aadhav sent me an audio file.

Not a song with hidden lyrics. A recording of the reading centre's first session in the community hall, made with permission for the volunteer archive.

Chairs scraped. Children argued about dragons. Mrs. Mary asked someone to return a pencil.

At the end, his voice said, “Thirandhuttom, Shreya. Namma library thirandhuttom.”

I listened twice, smiling.

Then my email notification appeared: an editorial internship had shortlisted me for a summer position in Bengaluru.

Different city. New expense. Another distance.

I looked at the audio message and the email together.

Our second beginning was about to need real practice.

pages.title: Learning to say it
pages.text:
Aadhav sounded pleased when I told him about the interview. Then he asked the question I hadn't expected.

“What part worries you most?”

“Kaasu. Naan nalla pannuvana-nu bayam. Apram unna miss pannradhu. In that order today.”

“Tomorrow's ranking may change.”

“Definitely.”

He helped me prepare answers without writing them for me. Sana found a friend who could explain affordable accommodation. Appa checked the stipend details.

I went into the interview knowing the opportunity could be good and still require practical questions.

When they asked whether I had any, I took out a list.

Sixteen-year-old me would have called that terribly unromantic.

pages.title: Learning to say it
pages.text:
Meanwhile, Aadhav joined his college's audio club. At a small event, the scheduled host got stuck in traffic. Someone asked him to introduce the performers.

He told me later that his first answer was no.

Then he asked for a written introduction and five minutes to practise.

“I did it,” he said, sounding surprised.

I sat up on my hostel bed.

“How did it feel?”

“Scary. Then ordinary. Then scary again when I remembered I'd done it.”

I laughed with him.

His confidence wasn't something I'd given him. It was something he was building, and I was lucky to witness it.

pages.title: Learning to say it
pages.text:
The first real argument of our second beginning was about a missed call.

Yes, again. Growth does not replace the syllabus; sometimes it gives you another attempt at the same question.

He forgot to tell me his club meeting had moved. I waited forty minutes.

When he called, I said I was angry without pretending to be fine.

He apologised without listing every reason I should understand.

“I'll put the change in my calendar as soon as it happens,” he said.

“Naanum fifteen minutes mela wait panni overthink panna maatten. Message illana, en velaiya paathukuren.”

A boundary. A repair. No dramatic breakup soundtrack.

pages.title: Learning to say it
pages.text:
Two days later, I forgot our call because I was finishing an assignment.

The universe loved educational demonstrations.

He sent one message, then went to dinner with friends. When I called back, he was available for ten minutes.

“I'm sorry,” I said.

“I know. Tomorrow?”

“Tomorrow.”

He wasn't punishing me by having an evening. I reminded the oldest, most anxious part of myself of that fact.

Afterwards I added our call to my calendar.

It felt strange that something so ordinary could help protect something so precious.

Apparently, romance could survive a reminder notification.

pages.title: Learning to say it
pages.text:
I got the internship.

A real offer, with a stipend, clear dates, and work that involved actual editing rather than unpaid errands disguised as opportunity.

Amma cried a little. Appa asked whether they provided lunch. Both responses were love.

Aadhav sent a voice note saying he was proud, then called when my schedule allowed.

“I wish we could celebrate in person,” he said.

“Enakkum dhaan. Nee pakkathula irundha nalla irukkum.”

We ordered the same cheap dessert in different cities and ate it on a video call.

His melted first.

“Long-distance disadvantages,” he declared.

I took an extremely unflattering screenshot with his permission.

pages.title: Learning to say it
pages.text:
Rohan helped me carry a carton to the hostel storage room before summer. A friend photographed us with the box and posted it to our class group.

Aadhav saw it through a mutual friend and asked who he was.

I answered plainly, including the old coffee date.

“You hadn't mentioned that part.”

“It didn't feel relevant until you asked.”

He was quiet, then admitted feeling unexpectedly jealous.

I appreciated the honesty. I also made something clear.

“Unakku doubt irundha pesalaam. Aana friends-a vittudu-nu solla mudiyadhu.”

“I don't want you to,” he said.

We kept talking until those sentences matched.

pages.title: Learning to say it
pages.text:
Aadhav apologised the next day for sounding suspicious.

“I compared myself with a photograph,” he said. “Bad research.”

“Very poor sample size.”

He laughed, then added, “I want to meet the people in your life when it happens naturally.”

“That I can do.”

Months earlier, I might have treated his jealousy as proof of love. Now I liked the apology better.

At dinner, Sana asked why I looked thoughtful.

“I'm discovering that healthy communication has fewer background songs.”

“More eating, then,” she said, moving the sambar bowl closer.

An excellent adjustment to the soundtrack.

pages.title: Learning to say it
pages.text:
Nila had her own difficult season. She failed an exam she had expected to pass and stopped replying properly.

I travelled home for a weekend and sat with her on the terrace.

“I thought you'd be busy with your grand romance,” she said, trying to sound amused.

“Nee en life-la side character illa, loosu. Nee Nila. Unakku separate importance irukku.”

Her eyes filled before she could make a joke.

We spent the evening planning the resit, ordering food, and saying very rude things about the question paper.

I told Aadhav I'd call Sunday instead.

He said, “Give her my best. Take your time.”

pages.title: Learning to say it
pages.text:
During that weekend, Nila asked whether we thought we would marry someday.

“Someday isn't a plan,” I said.

“Listen to you, sensible madam.”

“I still overthink messages. Don't worry.”

But the question stayed with me.

Aadhav and I hadn't discussed marriage. At nineteen and eighteen, we were barely learning how to plan a summer. Wanting each other did not make us ready for everything.

That night I told him what Nila had asked.

He said, “Un kooda oru future venum. Aana adhukkaaga namma ippo avasarapada vendam.”

I slept better after hearing it.

pages.title: Learning to say it
pages.text:
On the train to Bengaluru, I opened the blue notebook.

Between old project lists, I wrote a new sentence: Love is allowed to travel with me without becoming the only reason I travel.

Aadhav messaged a photograph of his semester timetable. Under it: Our next scheduling villain.

I sent my work hours.

We found one evening that matched.

Then I put my phone away and watched the landscape change.

For the first time, leaving for something I wanted didn't feel like evidence against staying in love.

The train moved forward.

So did I.

pages.title: The story I shouldn't have sent
pages.text:
The publishing office occupied two bright rooms above a stationery shop. My supervisor, Leela, gave me a manuscript and asked what confused me as a reader.

I expected a test of intelligence. She wanted attention.

“Don't show me how clever you are,” she said. “Show me where the story loses its way.”

Enakku avangala udane pudichiduchu. Konjam bayamum vandhuduchu. Apparently both feelings could share one office chair.

For three weeks, I checked details, wrote reader notes, and learned how much care hid behind a smooth paragraph.

Then she invited interns to submit an original piece for the imprint's online journal.

I knew exactly what I wanted to write.

pages.title: The story I shouldn't have sent
pages.text:
I wrote about the school reading room, the blue folder, and a boy afraid of a microphone.

The piece was good. That made what I did next easier to excuse.

I changed names and identifying details. I told myself it was fiction. I sent it to Leela without asking Aadhav whether I could use that memory.

Her reply was warm. She wanted to discuss publishing it after revisions.

I called him, excited, and read a passage aloud.

He didn't interrupt.

When I finished, the silence felt different from his ordinary quiet.

“Is that supposed to be me?” he asked.

pages.title: The story I shouldn't have sent
pages.text:
“Only partly. I changed things.”

“You used the video.”

I heard the problem then, but my pride reached the sentence first.

“Nobody will know it's you.”

“Aana enakku theriyum, Shreya. Adhu naan-nu enakku theriyum.”

The room seemed to shrink around my phone.

Aadhav wasn't shouting. Somehow that made it harder to hide behind feeling attacked.

“I told you because I trusted you,” he said. “Not because I wanted it to become your best scene.”

I stared at the manuscript on my laptop.

For the first time, I saw the person I'd edited out of my own justification.

pages.title: The story I shouldn't have sent
pages.text:
We ended the call before saying more hurtful things.

I walked downstairs and sat outside the closed stationery shop. Traffic passed. Someone laughed into a phone. The world was inconsiderately normal.

Sana called, and I told her what happened.

“Did you ask him?”

“No.”

“Then changing the names doesn't answer the actual question.”

En side-la yaaravadhu pesuvaangala-nu paathen. My friends had become terrible suppliers of convenient excuses.

Upstairs, I wrote to Leela asking to withdraw the piece from consideration because it used a private experience I didn't have permission to share.

I sent the email before I could improve my excuse.

pages.title: The story I shouldn't have sent
pages.text:
Leela replied the next morning.

Thank you for telling me before publication. We won't use this version. Let's discuss another subject.

No catastrophe. No career-ending thunderclap. Just a consequence I could handle, which made my earlier defensiveness look even smaller.

I messaged Aadhav: I've withdrawn it. You were right that I should have asked. I'm sorry I defended the story instead of listening to you. You don't have to reply tonight.

Then I left him alone.

An apology didn't entitle me to immediate comfort.

Understanding that was much less pleasant than writing a good apology scene.

pages.title: The story I shouldn't have sent
pages.text:
Aadhav called two days later.

“I don't want you to stop writing about your life,” he said.

“Puriyudhu. Un personal memories ellam enakku publish panna rights kedaichiduchu-nu artham illa.”

He breathed out.

“Yes.”

We talked about the difference between describing my feelings and revealing something he'd shared in confidence. If a future story drew closely on him, I would discuss it before submission, and respect a no.

There was no instant return to easy jokes.

We stayed on the call anyway, doing the slow work.

For once, the quiet wasn't avoidance. It was room to think.

pages.title: The story I shouldn't have sent
pages.text:
My replacement piece was about the reading centre's move. I asked Mrs. Mary and the families involved before quoting anyone, and left out the private parts of our history.

Thara insisted the dragon's public transport upgrade remain.

“Essential to the plot,” she said through her mother's phone.

Leela liked the revised piece. She asked me to sharpen the ending and remove a paragraph where I congratulated the adults too much.

“The children have agency here,” she said. “Let them keep it.”
