I rewrote it.

The story became better when I stopped treating everyone in it as material for my own growth.

pages.title: The story I shouldn't have sent
pages.text:
It was published the following month.

Aadhav read it and sent a photograph of the centre's new noticeboard, where Mrs. Mary had pinned a printed copy.

“Thara says her quote is the best part.”

“She is correct.”

Then he added, “Idhu dhaan un voice, Shreya. Unna madhiriye irukku.”

I read the sentence once and let it be enough.

Trust didn't return because my next piece was good. It returned through the smaller things afterward: asking, waiting, keeping something private when I said I would.

I could write a dramatic reconciliation.

Living a careful one required more attention.

pages.title: The story I shouldn't have sent
pages.text:
Near the internship's end, Leela asked whether I would consider applying for a junior role after graduation.

No promise of a job. A real possibility if a position opened and my work continued to improve.

I called home first. Then Nila. Then Aadhav.

He sounded excited, but distracted.

“Are you okay?”

“Yes. I have news too.”

He had been offered a place in a selective sound-technology training programme linked to his college, with a later placement opportunity in Pune.

For a moment, we simply looked at each other through the screen.

Two good doors. Different cities behind them.

pages.title: The story I shouldn't have sent
pages.text:
I smiled, and meant it.

Then, because we had promised to use actual sentences, I said, “Unakkaaga romba santhosham. Aana namma rendu perai ninaicha konjam bayama irukku.”

“Same,” Aadhav said.

We didn't solve the next several years that night. We asked when the decisions were due, what the programmes cost, and what each of us wanted if fear wasn't answering first.

His answer was sound.

Mine was stories.

Neither answer included giving up the other person.

Neither came with a guarantee.

Outside my window, Bengaluru traffic kept moving in several directions at once.

I watched it for a long time.

pages.title: Two tickets
pages.text:
Back at college, I built my final-year project around children's reading habits. Aadhav began his training alongside his coursework.

We were busy in specific, unglamorous ways. I transcribed interviews. He learned signal routing. Neither activity looked especially attractive on a video call.

One night I fell asleep while he described a technical problem. The next week he nodded off while I explained a footnote.

We apologised, then laughed.

“Maybe we need better opening hooks,” I said.

“Maybe namakku first thookkam venum.”

We chose sleep.

Our relationship survived this shocking lack of theatrical devotion.

pages.title: Two tickets
pages.text:
Our families began asking more practical questions about the future.

Lakshmi aunty wanted to know whether different cities would become permanent. Appa asked whether we'd talked about money. Amma asked whether we felt free to disagree.

Those were better questions than simply asking when.

I told Aadhav about them.

“We should answer for ourselves first,” he said.

So we made a shared document about visits, costs, work, and what we could realistically promise for the next year.

At the top, he wrote: Not a contract. Please do not stamp.

I added a blue heading out of tradition.

pages.title: Two tickets
pages.text:
The document revealed an uncomfortable truth: we'd been imagining different timelines.

I pictured two years of work before deciding where to settle. Aadhav assumed we'd aim for the same city as soon as I graduated.

Neither plan was wrong. Neither had been spoken clearly.

“I thought you wanted that too,” he said.

“Un pakkathula irukkanum-nu aasai irukku. Aana adhukkaaga endha job-naalum okay-nu solla mudiyadhu.”

He went quiet, then nodded.

“I don't want that either. I think I made a hope sound like an agreement.”

We changed the document.

It felt less romantic and much more honest.

pages.title: Two tickets
pages.text:
Then Appa received another uncertain work notice, and I panicked about being far from home.

I began searching local jobs I didn't want. Aadhav asked if I was choosing them because they suited me or because guilt was loud.

“Easy for you to say,” I snapped. “Your family has already planned around you.”

His face changed.

He had spent school years helping his mother recover. I knew better than the sentence I'd used.

“That's unfair,” he said.

I apologised before he had to list why.

Fear explained my sharpness.

It didn't make him responsible for standing still while it cut.

pages.title: Two tickets
pages.text:
Appa settled the matter unexpectedly over dinner.

“Apply for the jobs you want,” he said. “We'll discuss the numbers when there's an actual offer.”

“But if things are difficult—”

“Then we'll tell you. Don't invent our instructions for us.”

Amma nodded so firmly I knew they'd discussed this already.

I realised I was doing to them what I hated others doing to me: deciding what they could handle without asking.

Later I told Aadhav.

“Family resemblance,” he said gently.

“Konjam careful-ah pesu. En manasu ippo renovation-la irukku.”

He laughed, and I sent the applications.

pages.title: Two tickets
pages.text:
Nila passed her resit and secured a teaching placement.

We celebrated with roadside corn and a phone balanced against my water bottle so Aadhav could join for ten minutes.

“I expect both of you at my first school programme,” she announced.

“Will there be dragons?” he asked.

“Only in the staffroom.”

After the call, she looked at me thoughtfully.

“You seem less frightened all the time.”

“Not less frightened. More willing to ask what actually happened.”

She raised her corn like a toast.

“To actual information.”

An unusual blessing. A useful one.

pages.title: Two tickets
pages.text:
Aadhav's programme scheduled its final showcase during my project presentation week. He wanted me there. I wanted to go.

Dates mattum set aagala. Evlo aasai irundhaalum, calendar-ku adhellam puriyadhu.

For one evening, disappointment made us both quiet. Then we agreed that wanting support didn't mean demanding impossible travel.

Kavya attended his event and sent me a short recording with his permission. He watched my presentation rehearsal over video the night before mine.

I wore the earrings Amma had given me and kept the umbrella bookmark in my notes.

He sent one message before I began.

Take your time. They came to listen.

pages.title: Two tickets
pages.text:
My presentation went well. Not flawlessly. I lost my place once and answered one question with an honest admission that my small study couldn't settle it.

My supervisor nodded rather than looking disappointed.

Afterward, I listened to Aadhav's showcase recording. He explained a sound design choice clearly into a microphone, then thanked his team.

I cried a little in the corridor.

Not because I'd fixed the boy who once froze.

Because he had done a difficult thing himself, with practice and help from several people, and I remembered how much it had cost him to begin.

pages.title: Two tickets
pages.text:
The offers came three days apart.

A junior editorial role in Bengaluru for me after graduation. A training placement in Pune for Aadhav once his course requirements were complete.

Both modestly paid. Both worth considering. Neither designed by a romance novelist interested in convenient geography.

We read the terms separately, asked our questions, and talked about budgets.

“Unakku nijamave indha opportunity venuma?” I asked.

“Yes. You?”

“Yes.”

There was our answer, though it didn't feel simple.

We accepted our own offers.

Then we planned a visit we could afford, because a future also needed dates smaller than someday.

pages.title: Two tickets
pages.text:
Before my graduation, Aadhav came to Chennai for a day with tickets booked well in advance.

We walked through the campus, and I introduced him to Sana and Rohan. People became people instead of names on screens.

At lunch, Rohan and Aadhav argued cheerfully about a film's sound mix while Sana declared both of them wrong.

I watched, relieved by how ordinary it was.

Later Aadhav said, “I like your people.”

“Unakku avangala pudikkum-nu enakku theriyum.”

At the station, I kissed his cheek after asking, suddenly shy.

He missed his next sentence entirely.

Very satisfying character development.

pages.title: The road doesn't straighten
pages.text:
Graduation made Amma cry into a tissue she'd brought specifically for the purpose. Appa took photographs of everything, including an accidental twelve-second video of his shoe.

Aadhav couldn't attend because of an assessment. He called afterward, asked about the ceremony, and listened to Appa explain the shoe video as if it were an artistic choice.

I was disappointed he wasn't there. I was also happy with the people who were.

That balance had taken me years to learn.

When we packed my hostel room, I found the blue notebook under a stack of textbooks.

Its spine was coming loose.

pages.title: The road doesn't straighten
pages.text:
I took the notebook to Mrs. Mary during my last week at home.

She repaired it at the reading centre, now settled into a small donated room beside the community hall. The six-month arrangement had become a longer partnership through patient work by volunteers.

Nothing had been saved by one speech alone.

I liked seeing the evidence of everyone who kept showing up.

Mrs. Mary smoothed new cloth over the spine.

“You use this one a lot.”

“Yes.”

“Appo nalla thirakka mudiyanum,” she said. “We leave room for it to open.”

I watched her hands and thought that was good advice for more than books.

pages.title: The road doesn't straighten
pages.text:
My first month at work was humbling.

I missed a duplicated line in a proof. I misunderstood a deadline. I cried in a bathroom that had excellent acoustics for private despair.

Leela, now my manager, corrected the work without treating a mistake as my identity.

Aadhav called after dinner.

“Enna nambi hire pannittaangale,” I groaned. “I feel like a very convincing fraud.”

“Did they tell you that?”

“No.”

“Then maybe let them finish training the actual employee.”

I laughed reluctantly.

He didn't promise I'd be brilliant every day.

He stayed while I made tomorrow's checklist, then reminded me to eat something other than biscuits.

pages.title: The road doesn't straighten
pages.text:
Pune was difficult for him too.

His first shared flat had a unreliable water supply and a roommate who practised drums at morally questionable hours. The placement work involved carrying equipment as well as learning it.

“I thought I'd feel more grown up,” he admitted.

“I ate cereal from a saucepan yesterday.”

“That helps.”

We compared cheap recipes and complained about rent. Sometimes our calls sounded more like a household committee than a romance.

Yet when his laugh came through my earphones while I washed dishes, my rented room felt less strange.

I began to understand ordinary companionship as its own kind of luck.

pages.title: The road doesn't straighten
pages.text:
Then a photograph from his workplace travelled through our families.

Aadhav stood beside a young woman in formal clothes at a company celebration. An aunt asked Lakshmi aunty whether “something had been arranged.”

By the time the question reached me, it had acquired the confidence of confirmed news.

For thirty seconds, I was seventeen again.

Then I called him.

“Indha famous photo-ku oru explanation kuduppiya, sir?”

He looked baffled, then groaned.

“That's my supervisor's daughter. It was a group photo before someone cropped it.”

I asked for the full picture.

There were fourteen people and a very large cake.

pages.title: The road doesn't straighten
pages.text:
We laughed first. Then we talked about the more serious part.

“Have your parents discussed matches with you?” I asked.

“No. They know about us. Have yours?”

“Only questions. No plans.”

We agreed to speak directly if that changed. Neither of us could control every relative's imagination, but we could keep it from becoming our main source of information.

Aadhav sent the full photograph to his family group with a cheerful explanation of the work event.

I showed Amma.

She inspected the cake.

“Icing konjam jaasthi,” she said, as if that settled the matter.

The only investigation that survived the evening.

pages.title: The road doesn't straighten
pages.text:
Our next visit was cancelled when Aadhav developed a fever and needed rest.

The tickets were partly refundable. The hotel wasn't. I tried to sound kind and succeeded until I mentioned how much I'd planned around it.

“I know,” he said miserably.

I stopped.

“I can be upset about the situation without making you feel guilty for being ill.”

“Thank you.”

We rearranged what we could. I spent the weekend with Sana instead and sent him a book recommendation.

He slept.

Love was occasionally a cancelled reservation and the decision not to turn it into evidence.

pages.title: The road doesn't straighten
pages.text:
When we finally met, six weeks later, I worried it would feel awkward after so much anticipation.

It did, for approximately four minutes.

Then he spilled coffee on a receipt, I laughed, and we became ourselves.

We walked through a public garden and talked about things too ordinary for messages: the odd painting in his flat, my colleague's elaborate lunch boxes, the fact that Nila's students had discovered stickers as a bargaining tool.

“Unna kiss pannalama?” he asked, so softly that my answer came out softer still.

“Mm. Pannalam.”

It was gentle, brief, and followed by both of us smiling at the ground like complete beginners.

pages.title: The road doesn't straighten
pages.text:
We spent the rest of the afternoon in a bookshop, each choosing one book within a strict budget.

Aadhav picked a collection of essays on listening. I chose a children's story with an ending that made me cry between the shelves.

“Naan ippo tissues vaanganuma?” he asked.

“About my ability to cry in public? Long-established issue.”

At dinner, we discussed the next visit before the current one ended. A date, a likely cost, a backup if work changed.

It didn't remove the sadness at the station.

It gave the sadness somewhere sensible to sit.

pages.title: The road doesn't straighten
pages.text:
Two months later, my team lost a major project. Leela warned us that some temporary roles might not be renewed.

Mine was among them.

The future I'd worked so hard to reach suddenly looked pencilled in.

I called Aadhav from the bus stop, trying not to cry where everybody could hear.

He asked whether I wanted advice or company first.

“Company.”

So he stayed on the phone while buses came and went.

After a while, I said, “Now advice.”

“All right,” he replied. “Let's look at what's confirmed.”

For the first time that evening, the world became a size I could hold.

pages.title: The things we choose
pages.text:
My role would end in six weeks unless a new project was approved. Leela offered references and time for interviews.

I updated my portfolio, asked permission before including internal work, and made a budget that removed several comforting illusions about my snack spending.

Aadhav offered to lend money if I needed it.

“Thanks. First enakku evlo venum-nu paathukuren. Apram pesalaam.”

“Of course.”

I appreciated that he didn't turn helping into a way of taking charge.

Some evenings I wanted reassurance. Others I wanted silence and a film.

I began saying which one, and he began believing the answer.

pages.title: The things we choose
pages.text:
A job opened in Pune. Editorial assistant at a small educational publisher. Relevant work. Fair terms. Close to Aadhav.

I applied because it met my actual criteria, then became suspicious of my own happiness.

“Am I doing this only for you?” I asked.

“Would you consider it if I weren't here?”

“Yes.”

“Appo naan bonus-ah irukkalam, illa?”

“A very annoying bonus.”

“Comes with warranty limitations.”

I laughed and prepared for the interview.

For years I'd feared choosing love would mean losing myself.

Now the harder task was allowing two good reasons to exist together without distrusting both.

pages.title: The things we choose
pages.text:
The interview went well until they explained the role would include mostly sales administration, with occasional editing.

I asked follow-up questions. The job wasn't dishonest; it simply wasn't the work I wanted.

They offered it anyway.

For an afternoon, I considered accepting just to end the distance and uncertainty.

Then I called Aadhav.

“I don't think it's right for me.”

He was disappointed. He admitted that before saying, “Appo en address-kaaga indha job edukkadha,” he said gently.

I declined politely.

That night I missed him terribly.

Making a sound decision did not immediately make it a painless one.

pages.title: The things we choose
pages.text:
An independent publisher in Chennai offered a remote editing contract, initially for six months. The work suited me, and I could stay with my parents while saving money and applying for permanent roles.

It wasn't the neat career staircase I'd imagined.

It was a real next step.

I accepted after clarifying workload and payment dates.

Aadhav helped me pack during a visit we'd already planned. We wrapped books in old newspapers and argued about whether I needed three chipped mugs.

“One has emotional value.”

“All three have structural problems.”

I kept one.

A mature compromise, with a handle.

pages.title: The things we choose
pages.text:
Moving home felt like going backward until Amma asked me to help set up a proper desk.

“Un work-ku space panrom,” Amma said. “Unna thirumbavum school-ku anuppala. This is your desk, your work.”

Appa found a better chair. Nila brought a plant with survival instructions more detailed than most legal documents.

Aadhav joined a video call to admire the desk and criticise the cable arrangement.

I began editing the next morning.

Outside, the same vegetable seller called down the street. Inside, I worked on a new manuscript.

A familiar place could hold a changed person.

I hadn't believed that enough before.

pages.title: The things we choose
pages.text:
One evening, Aadhav sounded unusually careful.

“I was offered a transfer possibility,” he said. “Not confirmed. A Chennai team needs someone next year.”

My heart leapt so fast I almost missed the rest.

“The work interests me. But I need to compare the role properly. I don't want to move only because we're tired.”

I understood immediately, including the part of me that wished he wouldn't be sensible.

“Ask your questions,” I said. “Then tell me what you want.”

He smiled.

We had once helped each other's fictional characters catch trains.

This was harder and more useful.

pages.title: The things we choose
pages.text:
The transfer required experience he hadn't yet completed. At least nine more months in Pune, then a review. No guaranteed place.

We were disappointed together without accusing the calendar of personal malice for more than ten minutes.

After that, we planned the next visit and talked about my contract renewal.

“You know,” I said, “our story would be shorter if one of us had a private helicopter.”

“Budget-la oru night bus irukku. Adhu okay-va?”

“Depends on the legroom.”

He sent me a terrible drawing of a helicopter with a bus ticket attached.

I saved it beside the paper boat photograph.

pages.title: The things we choose
pages.text:
The real surprise came from my own work.

A manuscript I had helped reshape received positive feedback from its author, who recommended me for another project. My contract expanded into a longer role with regular pay and flexible location within agreed working hours.

I celebrated cautiously, having learned that good news didn't need exaggeration to matter.

Aadhav listened to the details, then asked whether I'd told my parents.

“Amma has already fed three neighbours.”

“Appropriate distribution policy.”

For the first time in months, I bought a new book without calculating what it would replace.

Then I bought one for him.

pages.title: The things we choose
pages.text:
We turned twenty-three and twenty-two on the same day that year.

Exactly one year apart. Still a fact relatives occasionally discussed as if we'd personally rearranged time.

Aadhav sent a photograph of one candle in a small cake.

“Budget?” I asked.

“Symbolism. You remain one candle ahead.”

I laughed so hard Amma asked what he had done now.

That evening, we talked seriously about the next few years. Marriage entered the conversation without either of us pretending it was just a joke.

“I want that with you,” he said.

“Enakkum venum. Namma rendu perum ready-aana apram.”

pages.title: The things we choose
pages.text:
We agreed readiness needed more than a romantic answer.

We discussed savings, work, family responsibilities, living arrangements, and the fact that neither of us wanted the other to become the automatic manager of every household task.

Aadhav admitted he was bad at remembering grocery basics. I admitted I avoided looking at bank statements when anxious.

Very seductive conversation. Truly.

But afterward, I felt closer to him than I had after many prettier evenings.

We weren't auditioning perfect versions of ourselves.

We were asking whether the real people could build a workable life.

The answer was becoming yes, with effort.

pages.title: The same city
pages.text:
Nine months later, the Chennai position became available.

Aadhav interviewed, compared the responsibilities, negotiated a realistic start date, and called me only when he had a written offer he wanted to accept.

“Naan Chennai-ku varen, Shreya,” he said. “Indha thadava return ticket thevai illa.”

I sat down on the edge of my bed.

“For the role?”

“For the role. And I'm very happy about the person in the city.”

“Good answer.”

“Practised for several years.”

I cried, then laughed at crying, then asked when.

For once, the date was a beginning that didn't require another goodbye immediately after it.

I wrote it in blue.

pages.title: The same city
pages.text:
He rented a room near his office with a friend from training. I was living with my parents in the same city and helping with household expenses.

Same city did not mean same street. Traffic still had ambitions of its own.

Our first ordinary Wednesday dinner took three bus connections between us.

We arrived tired and hungry, ordered too much, and spent twenty minutes discussing the menu after we'd already ordered.

“This is what we travelled years towards,” I said.

“Aama. Ippo extra chutney venuma, future philosopher?”

“Yes.”

He passed it across the table.

I liked that no suitcase waited beside his chair.

pages.title: The same city
pages.text:
We learned each other's daily habits, which distance had edited kindly.

Aadhav believed arriving five minutes early was arriving on time. I believed five minutes was a flexible cultural suggestion.

I liked talking immediately after work. He needed half an hour of quiet first.

Neither preference was a moral achievement.

We found a rhythm. He sent a brief message when he needed to decompress. I used that time to call Nila or take a walk.

I started leaving earlier for buses.

Daily-nu solla maatten. Let us remain faithful to the facts.

Love improved my punctuality; it did not perform a miracle.

pages.title: The same city
pages.text:
Our first same-city argument involved a Saturday I'd assumed belonged to us.

He'd promised to help Anu prepare for a school event during her visit. I found out when I suggested lunch.

“I thought we usually met Saturdays.”

“Usually isn't every Saturday.”

He was right, though his tone didn't help. My disappointment wasn't a booking confirmation.

We apologised for the sharp parts and made a habit of checking weekend plans on Wednesday.

Then I asked if Anu wanted help with her script.

Only after Aadhav asked her, she agreed.

Apparently she preferred editors who didn't call every second sentence “nice.”

pages.title: The same city
pages.text:
Anu's event was a debate about whether libraries still mattered.

She argued yes with terrifying confidence and included an example from our old reading project.

Afterward she said, “You two made a lot of fuss about books and then somehow dated.”

“History romba accurate-ah irukku,” Aadhav said.

I bought her a juice for not mentioning our handwritten notes in her speech.

She grinned. “I didn't know about those.”

I looked at him.

He looked at me.

Too late.

By dinner, Anu had requested a full archive, and we had declined with the unity of people defending national secrets.

pages.title: The same city
pages.text:
On a quiet Sunday, we visited the reading centre.

Thara was helping younger children choose books now. She remembered my dragon voice and asked if it had improved.

“No,” Aadhav said before I could answer.

Betrayal remained a theme.

Mrs. Mary let us help with repairs at a long table near the window. The room smelled of paper and ordinary afternoons.

I looked at him bending over a damaged spine, patient as ever.

The first thing I'd noticed hadn't disappeared.

It had simply become one part of a person I knew far better now.

pages.title: The same city
pages.text:
Revathi ma'am joined us later, carrying a stack of books she'd collected from colleagues.

“I hear you're both in Chennai,” she said.

“Yes, ma'am.”

“And still arguing about labels?”

“Professionally,” I said.

She laughed. We thanked her for the project, for the workshop recommendation, for taking our work seriously when we were students.

She waved away the idea that she'd planned anything romantic.

“Enakku books arrange panna help thevaipattudhu,” she said firmly. “The rest is your responsibility.”

Aadhav looked at me.

“Fair assessment.”

I smiled.

Some people open a door without deciding what you must find on the other side.

pages.title: The same city
pages.text:
That evening we walked to the bus stop under one umbrella, now large enough for two people who had learned how to share it.

“I've been thinking about telling our families we're serious about marriage,” Aadhav said.

My heart gave the old ridiculous leap.

“So have I.”

“Not announcing a date before we agree.”

“No.”

We discussed what we wanted: time to save more, a simple celebration, room for both families' concerns without handing them every decision.

Then I asked whether he was frightened.

“Bayam irukku,” he said. “Aana un kooda vaazhradhu pathi illa.”

I held his arm a little closer.

pages.title: The same city
pages.text:
Appa asked to talk with both of us over tea.

He didn't demand a salary performance. He asked how we handled disagreements and what happened if work took one of us away again.

“We'd discuss the actual choice,” I said. “We can't guarantee there'll never be another distance.”

Aadhav added, “We can agree not to decide for each other.”

Appa nodded slowly.

Amma asked whether we both knew how to cook more than two dishes.

Aadhav admitted three, if rice counted.

“It counts,” she said. “But please learn a vegetable.”

Our future received conditional culinary encouragement.

pages.title: The same city
pages.text:
Lakshmi aunty's concern was different.

“Will Shreya feel she has to take care of everyone because she's older?” she asked.

I appreciated the question more than she expected.

“Oru varusham perusa irukken. Adhukkaaga naan avanukku second amma illa,” I said gently.

Aadhav nodded. “We'll share responsibilities. She's my partner.”

His father asked about timing and expenses. We answered what we knew and promised to return to the uncertain parts.

Nobody gave a grand speech approving destiny.

They asked for another conversation after we'd made a realistic budget.

On the way home, I felt oddly relieved.

A future worth building could survive arithmetic.

pages.title: Ordinary, extraordinary
pages.text:
Nila announced her engagement before we announced anything.

I screamed so loudly Amma came from the kitchen holding a spoon like emergency equipment.

Nila had been seeing a colleague's brother for a year. I knew him, liked him, and still cried as though she'd suddenly emigrated to the moon.

“I'm getting married, Shreya. Not being erased.”

“Theriyum. Aana konjam azha vidu. Affection-oda drama panren.”

“Accepted.”

Aadhav helped us organise a small celebration. Watching him listen to Nila's stories, I felt grateful that loving him had never required becoming less hers.

Our lives were adding rooms, not closing doors.

pages.title: Ordinary, extraordinary
pages.text:
At Nila's engagement, an older relative asked Aadhav whether he minded me being a year older.

I opened my mouth, already assembling a presentation.

He answered first, calmly.

“No. We were born on the same date, one year apart. It isn't a problem for either of us.”

The relative tried another joke. Aadhav changed the subject without laughing at my expense.

Later I thanked him.

“You don't need to thank me for that.”

“I know. I'm doing it anyway.”

He squeezed my hand beneath the table.

Some declarations were useful precisely because they weren't loud.

pages.title: Ordinary, extraordinary
pages.text:
Our budget conversation became three evenings and one mildly heated debate about guest numbers.

I wanted a small celebration. Aadhav agreed, then discovered his definition of small included several more branches of the family tree than mine.

We compared lists rather than accusing each other of changing.

Some people would attend a ceremony, others a later family lunch. We agreed not to borrow money for appearances.

When the numbers finally worked, we ordered tea and sat in relieved silence.

“Very romantic spreadsheet,” he said.

“Blue headings.”

“Obviously.”

I leaned my head on his shoulder, and the future felt less imaginary.

pages.title: Ordinary, extraordinary
pages.text:
Then my grandmother fell and needed help recovering at home.

The fall was frightening, though her doctors expected a good recovery with follow-up care. Our family's attention shifted immediately.

I reduced optional commitments and helped Amma coordinate visits. Aadhav brought groceries when we asked and stayed away when Paati needed quiet.

He did not arrive every day to prove anything.

One afternoon, Paati asked why he peeled fruit so slowly.

“Slow-ah pannina nalla irukkum, Paati. Quality control.”

She laughed and told him to use a smaller knife.

By evening, she had decided he could visit again.

A more rigorous assessment than any interview.

pages.title: Ordinary, extraordinary
pages.text:
We postponed our next family meeting until Paati was settled.

Nobody treated the delay as a bad sign. Life had made a practical request.

One night, exhausted, I told Aadhav I feared becoming responsible for everyone's feelings forever.

“You don't have to tell each person the version that keeps them happiest,” he said.

“I know in theory.”

“En kitta first practice pannu. Unakku enna venum-nu sollu.”

So I admitted I wanted a weekend without plans, including ours.

He looked disappointed for a moment, then nodded.

“Take it.”

I did.

When we met the following week, I had more of myself to bring.

pages.title: Ordinary, extraordinary
pages.text:
Paati improved steadily and began issuing household instructions with familiar enthusiasm.

During one visit, she asked Aadhav whether he could make coffee.

“Yes.”

“Good coffee?”

“That remains under review.”

She supervised from her chair while I leaned against the kitchen doorway, laughing.

After he left, she said, “He doesn't pretend he knows everything.”

“Neither do I.”

She looked at me for a long, affectionate moment.

“Now, maybe.”

I accepted the criticism with the dignity available to someone whose grandmother had witnessed every version of her stubbornness.

Approximately none.

pages.title: Ordinary, extraordinary
pages.text:
Aadhav and I began discussing a home in concrete terms. Rent near a useful bus route. A desk for my work. Space where he could listen without disturbing neighbours.

We agreed that each of us would keep money we could access independently, alongside shared expenses. We discussed chores before romance could quietly assign them to me.

“Who remembers buying detergent?” I asked.

“Shared list. Whoever notices.”

“Aana yaar notice pannuvaanga? Adhaiyum decide pannalaam.”

He laughed, then understood why I wasn't only joking.

We made responsibilities specific.

Promises sounded better once they had verbs someone could actually do.

pages.title: Ordinary, extraordinary
pages.text:
One evening, he brought the old cream letter.

Not as a test. Not to compare me with the girl who wrote it.

“I found a better sleeve for it,” he said. “The paper was bending.”

I read it beside him, smiling at my seventeen-year-old handwriting.

“The actual irritating person,” he quoted.

“Still accurate.”

He leaned back, pleased.

I thought about the years we'd blamed that missing envelope for so much. Finding it had given us a conversation, not returned lost time.

We had built everything after that ourselves.

I was glad. I trusted what we'd built more than a miracle.

pages.title: Ordinary, extraordinary
pages.text:
I began writing this book a little before our twenty-fourth and twenty-third birthdays.

I asked Aadhav what parts of our fictionalised story he was comfortable sharing. In this telling, we could keep the emotional truth while choosing the details together.

He read the outline, suggested that my dragon voice deserved stronger criticism, and asked for some family moments to remain private.

I agreed.

“Are you finally going to reveal my name?” he asked.

“Eventually.”

“How eventually?”

“After one hundred pages.”

He stared at me.

“Shreya, oru introduction-ku nooru pages-ah? Konjam over illa?”

“You were worth introducing properly.”

pages.title: Ordinary, extraordinary
pages.text:
On our birthday, he handed me a small parcel.

I immediately looked suspicious, because months of practical marriage conversations had made small parcels emotionally dangerous.

“Open it,” he said, laughing.

Inside was a fountain pen. Deep blue. A note beneath it read: For all the pages after the ones we planned.

I loved it so much I forgot to be suspicious.

Then he added, “There's somewhere I'd like to take you next Sunday. If you're free.”

“The calendar has been consulted?”

“Thoroughly.”

I said yes.

For the next six days, Nila became extremely bad at changing the subject.

pages.title: A question with room for yes
pages.text:
Sunday began with rain, which at this point felt like a recurring employee demanding screen time.

Aadhav met me outside the reading centre after its morning session. The children had gone home. Mrs. Mary handed him the keys to lock up after our visit and reminded him about the side window.

No crowd waited inside. No hidden audience with phones.

Only the long table, a few books, and two chairs.

One had a familiar repaired leg.

“Idhu namma chair-ah?”

“Ma'am says technically it belongs to the school. She's lending it for the afternoon.”

I laughed, already close to tears.

pages.title: A question with room for yes
pages.text:
On the table lay a new blue folder.

Inside were photocopies of old project lists, a picture of Thara's first dragon drawing, and a blank sheet labelled What happens next?

I looked up at Aadhav.

“Namma future pathi neraya pesirukkom,” he said. “I know this isn't the first time you've heard what I want. I wanted to ask in a place where we learned how to do things together.”

His voice shook a little.

He didn't apologise for that.

I put down the folder so he could see he had all my attention.

pages.title: A question with room for yes
pages.text:
“I love you, Shreya,” he said. “The person you were, and the person you keep becoming. I want a life with room for your work, my work, our people, and whatever we haven't figured out yet.”

He opened a small ring box.

“Will you marry me?”

There was space around the question. We had discussed marriage already, but he still waited for my answer rather than reaching for my hand.

“Un kooda dhaan,” I said, crying now. “Enakku indha life un kooda dhaan venum. Yes, Aadhav.”

Then, because my personality had survived the occasion, I added, “But we are not keeping a wobbly dining chair.”

pages.title: A question with room for yes
pages.text:
He laughed so hard he nearly closed the box again.

“Agreed.”

The ring fitted, though my hands were shaking enough to make the process less graceful than advertised.

We hugged for a long time. When I stepped back, he brushed a tear from my cheek after I leaned into his hand.

“I had a whole sentence prepared,” I admitted.

“Enna sentence? Ippo sollu. Naan kekkuren.”

“I've forgotten.”

“Excellent. Now we both have evidence that you can run out of words.”

I kissed him, smiling.

Outside, rain tapped the window. Inside, nobody needed it to explain how we felt.

pages.title: A question with room for yes
pages.text:
We called our families first.

Amma cried. Appa asked whether we had eaten. Lakshmi aunty said she'd been waiting to hear our voices since morning. Anu demanded a clear photograph of the ring and warned Aadhav against blurry photography.

Then I called Nila.

She answered, “Finally.”

“You knew?”

“Only the place and time. I have suffered responsibly.”

I thanked her for keeping it private rather than organising a surprise crowd.

“Nee emotional-aana audience pudikkadhu-nu enakku theriyum,” she said. “Except me. Enakku lifetime licence irukku.”

I laughed through the last of my tears.

pages.title: A question with room for yes
pages.text:
When we returned the keys, Revathi ma'am was waiting with Mrs. Mary at the school office.

We told them together.

Ma'am looked delighted, then pointed at Aadhav.

“You did close the side window?”

“Yes, ma'am.”

“Good. Congratulations.”

Mrs. Mary hugged me and said she was pleased the blue folder had finally produced paperwork worth celebrating.

I thought about that first instruction: I need a favour.

A teacher had needed help with books. Two students had shown up, argued, grown, left, and returned.

It felt better than destiny arranging everything.

It felt like people taking care with what they found.

pages.title: A question with room for yes
pages.text:
Our engagement did not fix the commute.

The next Wednesday, my bus was late, Aadhav was hungry, and I arrived annoyed at a message he'd meant as a helpful update.

For five minutes we were two tired people with a ring between us and very little patience.

Then he asked, “First saapidalama? Apram konjam less angry-ah pesalaam.”

“Yes.”

We ate, apologised for our tones, and discussed the actual problem.

I was relieved, oddly, by the ordinary argument.

The proposal hadn't transformed us into a perfect couple we now had to impersonate.

We could still be ourselves and keep learning how to be kind.

pages.title: A question with room for yes
pages.text:
We chose a ceremony date far enough away to save comfortably and plan without turning every weekend into a crisis.

Our families helped. They also disagreed about flowers, food, and the correct number of people who could be described as essential.

We listened, made compromises we could afford, and kept a few choices firmly ours.

“No arriving on a horse,” I told Aadhav.

“Naan horse-ku application-ey podala.”

“Preventive communication.”

He nodded solemnly.

That evening we chose a simple invitation design with blue lettering.

Of course it was blue.

Some decisions had been made in a school workroom years earlier.

pages.title: A question with room for yes
pages.text:
My first children's book contract arrived while we were comparing invitation proofs.

I read the email three times before speaking.

Aadhav looked up immediately.

“What happened?”

I turned the screen towards him.

He read it, then grinned so openly I began crying again.

“Your own book,” he said.

There would be edits. Deadlines. Work I hadn't learned yet. None of that reduced the joy.

We put the invitations aside and bought cake.

“En train enakku kedaichiduchu,” I whispered.

He touched his forehead gently to mine.

“You always did.”

And I knew he meant the train was mine, not a gift he had permitted.

pages.title: A question with room for yes
pages.text:
The final unexpected turn came from Thara.

At the centre, she showed me a notebook filled with stories she'd written herself. On the first page was a dedication to everyone who didn't throw away books without endings.

I sat beside her and asked if she'd like me to read one.

She chose a story about a dragon who opened a repair shop.

Aadhav listened from the next chair, smiling.

For years I'd thought our project had given me my love story.

It had also given other people beginnings that had nothing to do with us.

That made the room feel wonderfully large.

pages.title: All the pages after
pages.text:
A few weeks before the wedding, I sat cross-legged on the floor with the blue notebook. Aadhav sat beside me, sorting invitation envelopes.

I found the first line I'd ever written about him: Annoying. Good at fixing things. Thinks alphabetical order is a personality.

“Enna review idhu?” he asked. “One star-ah?”

“Wait. There's more.”

Underneath, in smaller handwriting: He listened when I spoke.

His teasing expression softened. He took my hand and kissed the ink stain on my finger.

“Innum kekkuren,” he said. “Un stories ellam. Even the ones you haven't written yet.”

I leaned against him, my notebook open across our knees. Once, I'd hidden whole feelings between its pages. Now he sat close enough to read them, and I didn't want to close the book.

pages.title: All the pages after
pages.text:
With the school's permission, we visited the old reading room. The door opened smoothly now.

“No dramatic entrance available,” Aadhav said.

“En love story-ku maintenance department full damage.”

He laughed and stood where he'd once caught the dictionaries. I could almost see us: sixteen and fifteen, arguing about labels, with no idea how far a ten-minute favour could travel.

“Appove unakku enna pidichirundhudha?” I asked. Had he liked me even then?

“Appove nee thirumbavum varanum-nu nenachen.”

He'd wanted me to come back.

“Next Monday vara varaikkum romba long-ah irundhudhu,” he admitted.

All those years, I had thought I was the only one waiting for lunch.

I took his hand. “Naanum dhaan.”

We stood there smiling at the ordinary little table that had kept both our secrets.

pages.title: All the pages after
pages.text:
The night before the ceremony, Nila helped sort my earrings into little boxes.

“Bayama irukka?” she asked.

“Konjam. Mostly about tripping.”

“Un shoelace history paatha, reasonable fear.”

We laughed until I cried, then cried because laughing had loosened something tender.

I thanked her for every bus seat, every honest answer, every time she reminded me I had a life beyond waiting for a boy. She hugged me tightly.

“Nee happy-ah iru. Adhu podhum.”

My phone lit up beside us. Aadhav had sent a photograph of the old blue bookmark tucked inside tomorrow's clothes.

For stories with better endings.

Nila looked at it, then at me. “Okay. Indha scene-la naan tease panna maatten.”

For almost a full minute, she kept that promise.

pages.title: All the pages after
pages.text:
Amma came in after Nila went downstairs. She placed safety pins beside my clothes, then sat close enough for our shoulders to touch.

“Enna yosikkura?”

I admitted that I was happy, but a little frightened of how much tomorrow would change.

She smoothed my hair. “Ellame ore naal-la maari pogadhu, ma. Nee eppovum enga ponnu dhaan.”

I rested my head in her lap the way I had after difficult school days.

“You can always come home,” she said. “Santhoshathayum solla varanum. Not only when something is wrong.”

“I will.”

Downstairs, Appa was arguing gently with a delivery driver about directions. Someone laughed in the kitchen.

Tomorrow, I would make a home with Aadhav. Tonight, I let myself be held by the first home I had ever known.

pages.title: All the pages after
pages.text:
Aadhav called just before I slept.

“Thoongalaya?”

“Unakkum thookkam varala, illa?”

He laughed softly. Then the line went quiet in that comfortable way I'd once been too frightened to recognise.

“Naalaikku unna paakanum-nu romba aasaiya irukku,” he said.

“We met yesterday.”

“Theriyum. Aana tomorrow, when the photos are over and everyone goes home, I don't have to watch you leave for another city.”

My throat tightened. I had been thinking exactly the same thing.

“Enakkum adhu dhaan venum,” I whispered. “An ordinary evening. With you.”

“Ordinary evenings neriya irukkattum.”

We stayed on the call a little longer, saying nothing remarkable. When I finally closed my eyes, I wasn't imagining the ceremony.

I was imagining his slippers beside mine by the door.

pages.title: All the pages after
pages.text:
The ceremony morning was bright. After all that rain, the weather chose to mind its own business.

Appa fussed over directions. Amma checked the food. Anu guarded an emergency bag as if she had personally been appointed minister for safety pins.

Then I saw Aadhav.

He turned towards me and forgot the sentence he'd been saying. His eyes shone; his smile trembled at one corner.

“Nee azhariya?” I whispered when I reached him.

“Konjam,” he admitted. “Nee romba azhaga irukka.”

Suddenly I was the shy girl under the school verandah again.

He offered his hand. I took it, feeling his familiar thumb brush my knuckles.

Around us, people called out instructions. For one quiet second, we simply looked at each other.

Here, his smile seemed to say.

Finally, here.

pages.title: All the pages after
pages.text:
We married with our families close and enough little mistakes to keep the day human. A garland caught on a button. Someone misplaced a microphone. A child asked loudly when lunch would start.

Aadhav and I laughed together.

During a quiet moment, he bent close enough for only me to hear.

“Enna, senior? Indha junior-a lifetime tolerate panna ready-ah?”

“Oru condition.”

“Enna?”

“Orange sweets ellam enakku.”

He smiled. “Unakku dhaan.”

I squeezed his hand, suddenly unable to keep joking.

“Naan unnai romba nesikkiren, Aadhav.”

His expression changed at the sound of it. He lifted my hand and pressed a kiss to my fingers before answering.

“Naanum, Shreya. Romba.”

We had said it before. That morning, with his voice unsteady and his hand warm in mine, it felt new enough to make me blush.

pages.title: All the pages after
pages.text:
At lunch, Revathi ma'am sat with Mrs. Mary. Thara showed Nila her latest story. Kavya adjusted Aadhav's collar for a photograph, and I started laughing before she touched it.

“Old research error,” I explained to Anu.

Later, when the room grew noisy, Aadhav noticed me rubbing the little mark my earring had left.

“Konjam veliya varriya?”

We found a quiet stretch of verandah. He brought water and a small plate of the food I'd been too busy to eat.

“Bride-ku saapadu important illa-nu yaar sonna?”

I broke a sweet in half and offered him the larger piece.

“Unakku naan save panninen,” I said.

He smiled as he took it.

Between the blessings, the photographs, and the beautiful words, that little pause became one of my favourite memories: him noticing, me making room beside me.

pages.title: All the pages after
pages.text:
Our first quiet evening included missing spoons, a box labelled kitchen that contained only books, and takeaway dinner cooling on the floor.

Aadhav found the cream envelope while searching for plates. He sat beside me and read the last line again.

The actual irritating person.

“Innum same opinion-ah?”

I moved closer until my shoulder rested against his. “Adha vida konjam adhigam pidikkum ippo.”

He set the letter down carefully and tucked a loose strand of hair behind my ear.

“How much more?”

I kissed him instead of answering. He smiled against my lips, then kissed me back, gentle and unhurried.

We stayed there with our foreheads touching, laughing softly at nothing.

No train to catch. No call ending because a battery was low.

When he held me close, I could finally stop counting how much time we had left.

pages.title: All the pages after
pages.text:
So after a long time, we finally met. My one and only one, apdi nu dhaan solluven.

This time, no correction.

Aadhav looked over my shoulder as I wrote the last line.

“Book mudinjiducha?”

“The book. Namma story illa.”

He took the pen from my fingers and placed it safely beside the notebook. Then he held my hand between both of his.

“Shreya, un kooda irukkumbodhu dhaan veetukku vandha madhiri irukku.”

With me, he felt he'd come home.

I touched his cheek. “Enakkum dhaan.”

He kissed my forehead, then my lips, and I leaned into him without one thought about leaving.

The kettle whistled. Neither of us moved immediately.

“Tea?” he whispered.

“Innum konjam neram ippadiye iruppom.”

Just a little longer like this.

He drew me closer. “Evlo neram venumnaalum.”

I closed the notebook and rested my head against his heart.
